speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon, L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, as leader of the
house I should like to make a very short statement concerning a sensational story about a member of parliament published in the Telegram under date of yesterday, Wednesday, April 22, 1953. The story is headed "Government Contractor paid $71,800 to Liberal M.P."
I am sorry this story has come out at a time when the member concerned has had to return to Saskatchewan to the sickbed of his aged mother.
If he were here, I am sure he would be most anxious to deal with it at once as a matter of personal privilege and I hope he would be able to do so in a manner that would satisfy everybody as to the propriety of whatever he may have done. I am also confident that, if there remained anything which might be a cause of embarrassment, he would wish to take the steps required to prevent that embarrassment from being shared by anybody else. Until the hon. member has had an opportunity of dealing with this story, I think his fellow members and the public generally should keep an open mind about it.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN ANZUS PACT- STATEMENT IN NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question, to the Prime Minister. A press dispatch from New Zealand a day or two ago indicated that during a discussion in the New Zealand parliament one of the members had raised the question of Canada wanting to become a member of the ANZUS pact and being refused admission.
The minister of external affairs for New Zealand notified the house that that was not correct and is quoted as having said "Canada didn't want to be in." I should like to ask whether or not that explanation by the minister of external affairs for New Zealand is accurate.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN ANZUS PACT- STATEMENT IN NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I saw the Canadian Press dispatch in the Citizen of April 21. It was followed by a comment by the newspaper itself which I think states accurately the position. The comment was as follows:
Canada has always expressed "interest" in the ANZUS pact of Pacific powers but the Canadian government has never taken the view that this country should be a member although this has been urged in parliament here on several occasions by members of the official opposition.
External Affairs Minister Pearson has stated that if an invitation is forthcoming to join, it would then be considered. None has been forthcoming so far, and none is being sought.
That is exactly the situation.

maintopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN ANZUS PACT- STATEMENT IN NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT
speechtext: In fact the statement by the minister of external affairs for New Zealand is correct.

maintopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN ANZUS PACT- STATEMENT IN NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend can put any construction he likes upon the statement of the minister of external affairs for New Zealand. The fact is that no invitation has been forthcoming and none is being sought.

maintopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN ANZUS PACT- STATEMENT IN NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Would it be accepted if it were forthcoming?

maintopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADA IN ANZUS PACT- STATEMENT IN NEW ZEALAND PARLIAMENT
speechtext: The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) stated, and I think wisely, that that would be considered if and when it happened.

Mr. Chairman, last evening I was quoting a number of small passages from the excellent speech made by the minister on April 17 and I was referring to expressions used which I thought it would be in the interests of the committee and the country to have the minister elaborate upon or explain. In order to give continuity to my remarks, this morning I shall quote again the last passage which I quoted last night, which was from page 4067 of Hansard of April 17. I quote:
Canada and the United States have helped themselves and the world as a whole through the negotiation of extensive trade agreements, before the war in 1935 and 1938, and since the war under GATT at Geneva in 1947 and at Torquay in 1951. The unprecedented flow of trade between Canada and the United States today is conducted in accordance with the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
I asked the minister several questions, the first of which I shall repeat. I asked: Just how has Canada helped herself through GATT? At whose expense has Canada helped herself, if at anybody's? Just how has the United States helped herself through GATT and at whose expense, if anyone's? For instance, has this help in the case of one of these nations or the other been at the expense of Great Britain or some member of the British commonwealth? It would comfort us to be assured, and with proof, that such had not been the case.
Does the minister know who originated the idea that led to the instrument called GATT? Does he know what were the immediate objectives of the first movers in this con-

nection? For example, were the men who began this movement aiming directly at the destruction of imperial preferences and the pound sterling in the British commonwealth; in other words, not aiming at the welfare of the world at all but merely aiming at the opening of the markets of the British commonwealth to the United States? If that were found to be the case I think it would detract in some measure from the sanctity which is endeavoured to be cast about this whole GATT mechanism.
What were the ultimate objectives of this movement? For example, was it just to give the American people markets and to destroy the British commonwealth? I know it sounds harsh to suggest that a nation like the United States, that ought to be by far the most tenderly friendly nation towards Great Britain on the face of the earth, might be aiming directly at the utter destruction of the British commonwealth. I am afraid that some of the evidence available indicates that we had better not be quite too sure that she has not been seeking the dismemberment of the commonwealth, and is not now. By "she" I mean those who are deep in the American administration and are determining ultimate policy.
Does he know that the basic principle upon which GATT is founded is a fallacy, and that Samuel Crowther, in his excellent book called "America Self-Contained", makes remarks which indicate quite unanswerably that the belief in free trade is a myth, that there never has been free trade, there is not now free trade, and that with the world consisting of nations of such a wide variety of economies and economic strength it never can exist?
If this whole GATT idea is based on the ultimate validity of free trade, then this document is foredoomed to failure. Will the minister tell us what he knows about all this?
The next quotation from the minister's speech which I wish to read is to be found at page 4067 of Hansard of April 17, and is as follows:
Since the tariff undertakings of the general agreement on tariffs and trade are firmly bound only until the end of 1953, decisions will have to he made amongst the countries concerned as to what further steps to take to safeguard the future of international trade. There may be a further opportunity to take steps forward in the reduction of tariffs and the elimination of trade restrictions, as an alternative to moving in the other direction. The interest of Canada in this matter is perfectly clear, because we require other markets to be open to our goods on an expanding scale.
Before asking questions, I draw attention to the fact that the statement which I have
Supply-Trade and Commerce just quoted seems to be designed to give the idea that it would be impossible for Canada to get other markets and have an expanding scale of trade unless we have the mechanism called GATT. I might ask in a general way, how on earth did trade expand before men created GATT? I should like to requote the last sentence:
The interest of Canada in this matter is perfectly clear, because we require other markets to be open to our goods on an expanding scale.
What has caused our expanding trade up to the present time? It seems to me, as I will develop later, that in this part of the passage I have just read there is an attempt to arrogate, shall I say, to the mechanism called GATT credit for all expansion of trade and the development of resources and production which has taken place during recent years.
There are however several statements in the minister's speech to which in fairness I must refer, which indicate that the objective which I have suggested was not predominant in these two passages, but nevertheless I think what I have said has some justification. As examples of passages which show that the minister is aware that other factors have entered into the situation, we find the following quotation on page 4067:
That this is so is due primarily to the capacity and enterprise of the Canadian people and to the extent and variety of the resources which they have at their command.
That is quite correct. Again:
Government policies, too, have played an important role, and I wish to refer briefly to some of the trade promotional activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce, particularly to the work of the trade commissioner service which is well known to many of you in a general way.
Again:
-it was built up and organized on such a scale as to give Canada a really competent trade service in most of the world's principal commercial centres.
Again, in the next column:
It was Canada's rapid commercial growth that accounted for this marked departure from the ordinary sequence of events.
If the minister desired to emphasize those considerations which I have indicated in these later quotations, then he pretty nearly hewed out from under GATT all the credit which it would appear he attempted to give in the two major quotations which I gave at the beginning of these remarks.
I would say that the whole of the minister's April 17 speech, as recorded on pages 4063 to 4068 of Hansard, appears to have been designed to convey to the house and the country that the highly gratifying growth of Canadian trade and production is largely, if not mainly, a result of the general
4268	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce agreement on tariffs and trade, commonly called GATT, signed at Geneva in 1947, again at Torquay in 1951, firmly bound only until the end of 1953, and presumably desired by the present Canadian government to be signed again for another term of years.
Far too much credit appears to be sought to be given to the general agreement on tariffs and trade, far too much credit for the growth of our production and our trade. While other factors are by no means disregarded, there appears to be too little weight given to, first, the fact that we are at war or are in a war economy, a state of preparation for war, and the consequent physical and financial demands which naturally result from war. To give GATT credit for what is accomplished by being in a state of war preparation would certainly be obviously unrealistic. That is one of the kinds of thing to which I object. There appears to be too little weight given to, second, the richness and variety of our resources, which the minister mentioned in the passages I have quoted; third, the energy, resourcefulness and skill of our people, which the minister also indicated in the passages I have quoted; and, fourth, the growing industrialization of Canada.
Appropriate stress was laid by the minister upon what he calls "a really competent trade service in most of the world's principal commercial centres."
Nevertheless, all things being considered, his speech, whether intentionally or unintentionally, appeared to be, in effect, a propaganda speech, the over-all effect of which was to mislead the people in Canada and elsewhere, tending to encourage people to attach too much importance to, and place too much reliance in, GATT.
I should like to read a passage from the April 19, 1953, monthly bulletin of the Empire Industries Association and British Empire League. The passage, which I think has a message at this stage, reads:
A gradual reduction in American exports on an agreed plan plus a commercial agreement which would permit a reasonable use of both tariffs and preferences would do more towards closing the dollar gap and making convertibility possible than has been done by GATT in the past, or could be done by its continuation.
There is one element in that passage which I think ought to be modified to some extent and that is the statement that there should be a gradual reduction in American exports.
I do not agree with that particular part. I do not believe that there should be any gradual reduction in American exports but I do believe that American exports should not go into the economies of nations of the
[Mr. Blackmore.l

world, competing with the industries which those nations are endeavouring to establish. This latter kind of export of United States goods, which other nations of the world do not wish, would be forced into the economies of those nations to their detriment, whereas by rights those surplus American goods should be made available to the needy peoples of the world.
Once more may I say, Mr. Chairman, in all earnestness to the minister, that we in our generation simply must discover the means whereby we can take surpluses from our splendidly blessed countries and get them into the hands of the 1,400 million people who go to bed hungry every night. If we do not do that we will betray our trust in these generations in which we live.
One of the serious difficulties in respect of all proposals which emanate from the United States and Great Britain is that we find no indication whatever of their awareness of the urgent responsibility to get our surplus goods into the hands of needy people. I shall probably have more to say about that at a later time. As I see it, there is no escape from this responsibility, and so I would say that the surplus goods of the United States call for a means to be adopted whereby those goods can be put into the hands of needy people and not be thrust into the economies of other nations to the injury of the economies of those nations.
With these reservations I would say that the quotation which I read from the periodical issued by people who are realistic in all matters pertaining to trade is highly commendable, and I would suggest it as a sort of ideal to aim at as an alternative to GATT.

Mr. Chairman, during the debate yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton made quite a thorough and comprehensive speech on trade, along with various other matters. He referred to the fact that Canada as a whole had been doing a fair job of selling surplus products with the exception of certain farm products which were not now going to Britain, such as bacon, cheese, et cetera. Mr. Chairman, I think it can be said without contradiction that at the present time the only surplus products we have in Canada are a little canned pork and possibly a few dairy products.
What?

The reason for those surpluses is mainly the embargo which was placed on certain products because of the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak last year.
What the hon. member for Eglinton forgot to say was that Britain is able now to

purchase many of those products at a figure much lower than that at which our products are selling at the present time in Canada and in the United States. Take for instance beef which would cost Britain 35 cents per pound today if she were to buy from Canada. She is able to get Argentine beef laid down in Britain at the present time for 17 cents a pound. Suppose the wife of the hon. member for Eglinton were to ask him to bring home some meat for the daily meals. If there were three stores such as Loblaw's, A. & P., and Dominion Stores, and if two stores were selling meat at 40 cents a pound and the other selling it at 17 cents a pound, there is no doubt that even the member for Eglinton would stretch his dollar by purchasing in the cheaper market. I believe that the reason for Britain's hard dickering today is the dollar shortage. Despite the dollar shortage in Britain our government has done very well up to the present time in disposing of surpluses to other markets and, owing to the trade minister's mission to South America, we have found outlets for much more of our production.
Mr. Chairman, in listening to the somewhat lengthy statement of the leader of the C.C.F. party, and I see he is in his seat now, I was shocked to learn that he did not know why Canada's dollar was at such a premium today.
You tell us.

I am sure that it was a
terrible blow to members of that party to find that their leader did not know the answer to that question.
Well, you tell us.

I am sure that it will be a
severe blow to those who support the C.C.F. in Canada to discover that a man aspiring to the leadership of the C.C.F. in Canada does not know why Canada's dollar is at such a high level. Most assuredly such a man cannot be considered too seriously by the people of Canada.
You tell us.

I will give you my own
opinion when we get into finance.
Oh, oh.

I did not interrupt the hon. member yesterday and I hope that he will be gentleman enough not to interrupt me today.
I rise to speak today because of the failure of Britain up to now to sign the international wheat agreement. I think that it would be
Supply-Trade and Commerce a tragic mistake if we did not give Britain some inducement to enter into this agreement. During the war we lent Britain $1,250 million and then made a straight gift of $1 billion. Those were steps in the right direction in order to enable Britain at that time to buy much of the produce produced in Canada. Owing to her hard-pressed economy and preparation for this cold war Britain has rationed her people more severely than she did at any time during the last war. Owing to the very severe dollar shortage there is no question but what at the present time she is fighting for her very life and attempting to obtain cheaper food for her people.
And shorter hours.

Mr. Chairman, it would be a calamity for the British empire if Britain were not to join this wheat agreement. It would also be a severe blow to Canada. If I am not correct in making this statement possibly the minister can answer later, but I think I am right in saying that Britain would sign at a figure of $2 a bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is a resolution on the order paper having to do with the wheat agreement which I hope will be debated next week, perhaps early in the week. I think it would be much wiser not to discuss the wheat agreement at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order raised by the minister is well taken because, as the hon. member knows, we cannot anticipate discussion on a matter which is already on the order paper and which will come up later. Therefore, I will ask the hon. member to reserve his remarks on the wheat agreement until later.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I believe that the minister has good reason for saying what he has said, and I believe there may be good reason for some further negotiations before the deadline. In view of what the minister has said, I shall withhold my remarks until some future time.

I followed with considerable interest the over-optimistic remarks of my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce in introducing his estimates. I agree that Canada does enjoy an enviable position as a trading nation today. I think that Canada, with her undeveloped natural resources, should enjoy great prosperity in the future. We have huge resources of oil, iron ore, nickel, uranium, copper, pulpwood, lumber and many other very useful materials. We should be very proud to possess these resources. We have also a very industrious people in this nation, and that is all to the

Supply-Trade and Commerce good. Coupled with all this, we have had a great period of inflation. I believe it is acknowledged by our financial experts that the Canadian dollar now has a value of about 49 cents, and that should be taken into consideration in assessing these various matters. It does make a great difference to many people in this country of ours today.
While this country as a whole has enjoyed great export trade and prosperity, I am sorry to say that the same cannot be said of the farming population in this nation. They are in a very different situation. I feel in the past a greater effort should have been made, realizing that trade is a two-way street, to purchase from Great Britain more items needed for our defence program, such as tanks, airplanes and things that are in short supply for our armed services. Since the same minister is responsible for making these great expenditures, he should have exerted a greater effort to buy from Great Britain, thus making it possible for Great Britain to purchase more of our agricultural production. It goes without saying that we have lost a great deal of these overseas markets for products which have been mentioned such as apples, vegetables, meat and many other items. We did enjoy a good market for a number of those items, and those markets have been lost. I feel that the government has not put forth the effort that might have made it easier for Britain to purchase these things by supplying the equipment we need so greatly for our armed services at this time.
I think we have missed the boat in that respect. I do not think our farm population has ever been taken care of too well. According to the 1951 census there is 20 per cent and a fraction of the population located on farms in this country, and they only received 12 per cent and a fraction of the national income. In 1952, the agricultural statistics show that that income was reduced by 12 per cent, while the cost of farm production had increased by 5 per cent. This disparity is increasing day by day. Inflation is also increasing in this country, despite the fact that ministers say it has been checked. During the last month an item which certainly enters into western farm production costs, that is freight rates, was increased. The Minister of Transport admitted that this would have an inflationary tendency at this time. This is one item which enters particularly into western farm cost accounting. I say, therefore, that the farm population does not appear in this rosy picture painted by the minister.

It has been pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture and others-in fact by the hon. member for Springfield, who just resumed his seat-that the only surpluses about which we have to worry are canned pork and frozen beef. Last evening the member for Eglinton put on the record the amount of wheat now held by the principal exporting nations of the world. I have in my hand a bulletin on grain stocks held in Canada as of March 31, 1953. The dominion bureau of statistics, in co-operation with the statistics branch of the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada, has compiled this data. The total holdings in Canada as of March 31, 1953, are as follows: Wheat, 604 million bushels; oats, 309 million bushels; barley, 217 million bushels; rye, 22 million bushels; flaxseed, 7 million bushels. Those are the round figures, and there are some odd thousands to add. This statement shows that the average for 1943-52 is as follows: Wheat, 380 million bushels; oats, 223 million bushels; barley, 104 million bushels; rye, 9 million bushels; flaxseed, 7 million bushels. I would think that, apart from flaxseed, there is a great surplus shown by those figures. I believe that this is a cause for considerable concern amongst the grain producers of this country at this time.
I agree also that it is quite difficult for the minister to announce the initial payment that will be paid for grain produced for the crop year 1953. Such an announcement was made last year before seeding operations commenced, and we had hoped that in each year these initial payments might be announced as a guide to those who are planning their seeding operations. I hope the minister can announce those payments as soon as possible, because some farmers might want to make some shifts, although I agree that it is difficult under the prevailing conditions at this particular time.
With respect to the international wheat agreement, the minister has stated that we will be asked to discuss and ratify it at a later date, so I shall not go into any details on that. Much of the publicity concerning the agreement has been painting a very rosy picture, but I am afraid the results will be disappointing to the wheat producers of this country. It is understood that we shall have to ratify the agreement and there will be a debate then, but I should like to point out to this house and to the country that, in view of the stand taken by Britain, I do not believe we will definitely know what the position will be until after July 15. In answer to a question about the stand of the United States, the minister has pointed out that in all likelihood we shall have to take

a second look at this agreement following July 15 to see what can be done about quotas. The final position may be quite disappointing because, although all we read about in the newspapers has to do with the maximum price of $2.05, people are greatly concerned about the minimum price of $1.55.
I do not wish to deal in detail with the agreement at all, but I did want to point out that situation. I think we should be giving it serious thought before we are called upon to ratify the agreement.
According to the report of the Canadian wheat board for 1951-52, which is the last official record we have, as a result of the operations of the international wheat agreement there was a difference between the average prevailing price for class II wheat and what the farmer actually received of 48 and a fraction cents a bushel, which amounted to $140 million on all the wheat included in that agreement. There was a considerable loss on that basis in every year of the agreement. Of course it is all water under the bridge as to the many hundreds of millions of dollars that the producers had to forgo in order to carry out the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. They have had to make a great contribution. With respect to the price of domestic wheat in this country, may I say that I think it is unfair that the minister and his department, through the Canadian wheat board, should insist that the wheat producers of the prairies should continue to subsidize all the consumers of this nation to the extent that they do, because they purchase all their wheat on the basis of the international wheat agreement. I wish again to raise objection to that procedure and I hope that that will not be the case in the handling of wheat in the next crop year after August 1. I hope that discrepancy will be done away with.
I also want to repeat that on March 17 I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he would refer this report of the Canadian wheat board to the standing committee on agriculture, and he said he had no objection at that time if they wished to consider it. Mr. Chairman, you know how all the committees of the House of Commons are organized. The majorities in these committees are members of the government. It is true enough that you are perhaps supposed to persuade the chairman to call a committee, but there were many matters of concern which we could have discussed had the minister referred this report to the committee and had they sat. There were many matters that could have been discussed, including not only the handling of our grain but other
Supply-Trade and Commerce problems dealing with the Department of Agriculture as well. I am greatly disappointed that the committee has not been called. I noticed a press account one month later-I think it was last Friday or Saturday-to the effect that the chairman was going to poll the members of the committee and find out whether they wished to sit now and consider the report. I have pointed to the composition of these committees, Mr. Chairman; and I do not presume that, in this rush to finish up the business of this session, they will now sit. Certainly if they were going to do so, they should have met long before this, in view of the fact that this session of parliament opened last November.
I hope to have a great deal to say with respect to this international wheat agreement. I just wanted to register my disapproval of the fact that a greater effort had not been made to regain these markets for the agriculturists throughout this nation and also to point out the great disparity that exists between the position of these people and others of this nation at this particular time.

Mr. Chairman, I shall detain the committee for only a moment or two, but there are a few remarks I should like to make to the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he wants to listen to them particularly or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I must.

Despite the statement which he made last Friday night-which was an optimistic one-I think there are some obvious weaknesses in his trade policies. I think probably the foremost one is the fact that he, in conjunction with the United States, has done little in an economic way to strengthen the NATO treaty alliance. As I understand it, our foreign policy is based largely on NATO. The objective of that organization is the building of a strong defensive alliance against communism. We have gone a long distance, in a political and military way, to strengthen NATO, but I think we have fallen down badly in an economic way; and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce must accept ia good deal of responsibility for that fact.
Article 2 of the NATO agreement calls for economic co-operation. Yet both Canada and the United States have refused to make it easy for our European allies to sell their products and merchandise on the North American continent. I cannot see how the NATO alliance can be a really integrated community unless there are greater economic

Supply-Trade and Commerce ties. I think the absence of those ties can undermine the military aspect of the alliance.
What exactly is this country doing today? On the one hand, it is sending military forces overseas, and giving huge financial assistance to defend western Europe against communist aggression. Then on the other hand it is following shortsighted fiscal, economic and tariff policies which are tending to prevent our allies from working out their own economic salvation. I suggest that the time has surely come when Canada should make it easier for our NATO partners to send their merchandise within our borders.
I want to agree with many of the members who have already spoken about the British-Canadian trade impasse. We have reached the point where our farm products are simply not being sold in Britain, with the possible exception of wheat; even that market we may ultimately lose. Harsh economic realities are forcing the British to buy farm products from those countries that are buying from her. It is quite true-as the minister has pointed out-that we have found an alternative market in the United States; and I think most farmers and Canadians are grateful for that fact. But we know that in the past the American market has not been a stable one. We know that it has been subject to recessions, and particularly to changes in tariff policy. Even at this moment the farm bloc in the United States is agitating for higher tariffs against our meat and our coarse grain.
I think we must face the fact that if there are surpluses in the United States, Canadian farm products in the near future may face exclusion from that market. Under these circumstances Canadians must realize that it is not only vital but a matter of absolute self-preservation for us to regain our British markets for farm products. I think failure to do so may mean that, in the next decade, a great many farmers may face financial ruin. I say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, knowingly or otherwise, has led Canadian agriculture, within the last few years, down a kind of blind alley. We had better get out of that blind alley before it is too late.
What can be done to improve British-Canadian trade relations? I believe there is a great deal that could be done on both sides of the ocean. I think the first step must be taken by the British themselves. British manufacturers simply must become more aggressive in the Canadian market. Certainly any business experience I have had with the British leads me to believe that 

they today are not doing all they could to get into our market here in Canada. Many Canadian would-be buyers of British goods have recently been bewildered by the offhand manner of British manufacturers. The British tell us, "If you do not buy from us, we cannot buy from you." Yet when Canadian buyers-and I include myself- genuinely try to buy British goods, they are finding it virtually impossible in many lines. Among British suppliers one often finds interest that is lukewarm or condescending, prices that are vague, delivery dates that are uncertain, and styles and models that are not suitable for the Canadian market.
Several months ago dealers from all over Canada met in the city of Toronto at the annual Canadian hardware show. In that automotive building were display booths for goods from many parts of the world including Britain, Germany and many other countries. Many hardware dealers went down there with a specific desire to buy British goods. I know that my own company had two buyers who wanted to buy British cutlery, British tools, British shelf hardware and the like. However they obtained little satisfaction from the British suppliers on that occasion and ended up by buying German goods. It may be that our company is too small for these suppliers to bother with it; but I would point out that there were hundreds of other small dealers in a similar position who were leaning over backward trying to buy British goods at that fair. Yet in many cases they found it impossible to do so.
Speaking of the hardware business, may I say that before the war we handled little else but British cutlery. We handled a great many British tools, British toys and a great deal of British chinaware. We should like to get such merchandise again; but no matter how hard we try, we are finding it extremely difficult to do so. I would tell my British friends that today there is a crying demand among hardware dealers, from one end of this country to the other, for British cutlery, British scissors and British iron and steel goods. Where can we get such merchandise?
I ask British manufacturers what exactly is; wrong. Sometimes I wonder if they really want to get into this Canadian market. Those of us who live on the prairies want to sell our farm produce to Great Britain. We know that it is common sense and good business for us to buy British goods in return, so that they can earn Canadian exchange.
The Saskatchewan government not long ago set up a special committee whose duty

it was to encourage a "Buy British" campaign. The Hudson Bay association, the Coops and other groups, have also sponsored "Buy British" campaign. Thus it seems unfortunate that today, for one reason or another, many lines of British goods are not yet available. I do not make these comments in a critical sense at all, but only in the hope that our British friends will realize that there is much they themselves can do to improve British-Canadian trade relations.
I think the British should realize that since 1945 they have failed to take advantage of the tariff concessions which we have given them. Time and again British products have enjoyed tariff advantages over products from the United States. Yet, invariably the British products have been swamped by American competition.
Today where tariffs apply, the British rate is usually about 10 per cent lower than the American. For example, let us consider the drug and chemical industry. The tariff on those products, for British goods, is about 15 per cent less than the tariff on similar American goods. Yet of the $200 million worth of those goods which Canada imported last year, Great Britain got $20 million and the United States $175 million. Then, Canada imports more than $20 million worth of coloured cotton fabrics each year. The duty on the British fabrics is 3 cents a pound less than that on the American. Yet the United States factories got nine-tenths of the business last year.
In the field of iron and steel products the picture is much the same. The British enjoy a tariff protection or advantage of about 10 per cent. Yet last year imports from the United States were valued at $1-2 billion while the imports from Great Britain were valued at only $130 million. I have spoken to many buyers who have gone to Great Britain in an endeavour to buy British goods. Sometimes they were successful; but many times they found it virtually impossible to obtain the supplies they wanted.
I repeat that I am not saying this to belittle British efforts in any way; I am saying it because I realize how vital it is for my province and, I suggest, for the whole country, to increase British imports. But it has got to work both ways. The British, as well as ourselves, have to co-operate. It seems to me there are a number of steps the British could take if they really desire to sell more goods in Canada.
First of all, I think they should send out a far greater number of salesmen to this country to directly contact Canadian importers and businessmen. Secondly, I think they should
Supply-Trade and Commerce increase their advertising of British goods in this country. Thirdly, I suggest they should speed up delivery dates, and make those delivery dates specific, so that one could count on them. Fourth, I think they should give a greater degree of priority to the Canadian market. Fifth, I believe they should set up a more efficient system of spare parts and supplies in Canada. A great deal could be done by the British themselves to increase and improve British-Canadian trading relations.
Then, I believe a great deal more could be done by this government, if it were so inclined. For instance, I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce should set up an import committee, or a special branch within his department to encourage imports, particularly from the sterling area.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have had that special branch for years.
Well, it must be very inactive.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is very active.

I doubt it. Perhaps the
minister should have that branch of his department get in touch with importers, and tell them how essential it is for this country to buy British goods.
It is essential for the government to do a public relations job in this connection. And secondly, as other hon. members have suggested, we should increase our defence purchase orders in Great Britain, assuming always that prices are competitive.
In the third place, I believe our crown corporations, such as the Canadian National Railways, the post office, Trans-Canada Air Lines, Polymer and others should be requested wherever possible to give a preference to British goods.
In the fourth place we should consider at this time the feasibility of making further tariff concessions to the British.
In the fifth place I believe members of the House of Commons, and particularly ministers of the crown, should travel from one end of the country to the other making speeches, pointing out to our people why it is desirable and necessary for us to trade with Great Britain-not primarily for any reasons of sentiment, but solely for reasons of our own economic self-preservation. The time is past when the government, and particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce, can maintain an attitude of aloof detachment from the gravity of this trade problem.
The Canadian primary producers are calling upon the government for action. We think the only answer to the British-Canadian trade impasse is a "Buy British" campaign.

Mr. Chairman, may I first of all express to the hon. member for Peace River my appreciation of his relinquishing his time so that I might proceed. Duties which I have undertaken in connection with the work of the House of Commons have made it impossible for me to be present on most occasions when the house is sitting. It will be impossible for me to be here either this afternoon or this evening because of those duties. Therefore I appreciate the courtesy that has been extended to me.
Recently, and for a period of time, remarks have been made both in and out of the house which have been derogatory, to a large extent, of an industry in my constituency. Therefore I should like to say a word or two concerning the automobile industry in Canada, and particularly deal with the manner in which it affects the people of Canada, and our economy. I shall refer to its effects on the farmer on the prairies, the logger in British Columbia, the fisherman in the maritimes, as well as the workman in the factories of Ontario and Quebec.
I am, Mr. Chairman, not unconscious of the fact that I am speaking for the rank and file of the little people of my own constituency, four-fifths of whom are engaged directly or indirectly in the manufacture and assembly of automobiles, or the parts and accessories that go into the production of the automobiles. Of that four-fifths, three-fifths of my people are engaged in the direct manufacture and assembly of automobiles with the Chrysler, Ford and General Motors corporations, in chief, and the other one-fifth of the four-fifths are working for the some fifty odd feeder plants in my city.
The other main centres for the production of motorcars are presently at Oshawa, Ontario, where two-thirds of the population work for General Motors, and the feeder plants situated there, and at Hamilton, Ontario, where the Studebaker Corporation now produce motorcars.
In Canada there are now four companies which produce passenger cars and trucks. Then, of the aforementioned, there are two companies which produce passenger cars only. There are also four companies which produce trucks and buses exclusively. This is apart from the companies which import complete vehicles from the United States and the United Kingdom. These latter maintain some type of distribution facilities but are not regarded as a part of the automotive industry in Canada.
The first automobile produced in Canada was manufactured in Windsor, Ontario, in the year 1904, almost fifty years ago. There


were imported models, or horseless carriages, introduced to our country before that date, but the more advanced motorcar came to Canada from the United States through Windsor in the year aforementioned.
The 1904 model was a crude creation in comparison with the sleek, comfortable and speedy models of 1953. When one looks back at the improvements that have been made in the last 50 years one cannot help but think of what the next 50 years will bring in the way of jet propulsion or atomic energy as applied to the automotive industry. We in Canada can be sure that when these means have been developed to the proper stage the ingenuity and progressiveness of the automobile industry in Canada will adopt such advancements as may be applied for the full benefit of Canada and Canadians.
I am sure that in 1904 that small carriage company at Windsor, the manufacturer of the original motorcar, little realized that in 50 years the industry which they were getting under way would grow to be the second largest in Canada, second only to the pulp and paper industry as an employer of people and in the total wages and salaries paid. In 1952 the total value of the products of the automotive industry, including vehicles and parts, was estimated at $717 million. Little did those pioneers realize in 1904 that within 50 years there would be at a given time over three million motor vehicles on the roads of Canada and that those vehicles would represent an investment by their owners of more than $4-5 billion. That investment is greater than the total value of all lands, buildings, implements and livestock in the agricultural industry in Canada.
In 1952 automobile firms directly employed over 35,000 men and women with wages amounting to $132 million. Indirectly employment was given through 350 feeder plants to
148,000	persons who were paid $112 million. Those people were employed on automotive contracts during the period 1951-52. With the phenomenal growth of industry in Canada it is reasonable to expect that this industry will increase correspondingly in the years to come.
I have said that the industry was concentrated in Windsor, Oshawa and Hamilton, Ontario, but those are only the places where motorcars are manufactured. Oakville, Ontario, will soon become one of the leading centres in Canada for the assembly of motorcars. The whole economy of the country is supported by this industry. We must realize that it provides a market for the products of mine, forest and farm throughout the whole country. I regret that I have not available the amounts spent directly by the automotive

industry on subsidiary industries and feeder plants, but I do have the information given by the president of one company to a group of members of this house in this building early this year. He indicated the amount which his company had spent in the various industrial centres in 1952. It must be remembered that there are four companies manufacturing motorcars, as well as other companies producing trucks and buses, so it will be seen what this means to the industrial life of our country and to the many industrial centres represented by members of this house.

These are only a few of the leading towns in Ontario and Quebec which have benefited directly from this industry. Altogether there are between 350 and 400 communities in Canada which share in the business created by this industry.
Apart from the independent garage men and dealers in imported cars there are 5,200 automobile dealers in Canada selling cars and trucks under licences from the manufacturers. These dealers employ about 55,000 persons who are paid over $132 million a year in wages and salaries. If we were to group all the automotive industry together, that is the manufacturers and the people who work in the factories, the feeder plants with all their employees and workmen, and the dealers with all their salesmen and mechanics, we have an industry employing
238,000	men and women with a combined payroll of over $376 million. That is over $1 million per day which goes into the pockets of Canadian labourers, clerks and technicians.
This is not the only contribution made by this industry to the economic welfare of Canada. The demand for certain types of steel has led to the establishment of facilities for the production and processing of such steel in Canada. This steel need not be imported by other users as it is made available to the manufacturers of other commodities. With the development of Canada's vast iron ore resources, the establishment of these and other steel processing plants and the knowledge derived therefrom will be of immeasurable benefit in the future industrial growth of our country.
This industry is highly competitive and as such engages the most highly trained personnel, engineers, draftsmen, tool makers, accountants and highly-qualified office
Supply-Trade and Commerce workers. It is a magnificent industrial training ground and a leader in developing and adopting new methods and techniques which will facilitate higher and higher production with lower and lower costs.
This know-how and technique is available for the defence of Canada in time of war. This was proved during world war II. The knowledge of means and methods of mass production enabled the industry to turn out hundreds of thousands of motorized units for our armed forces. It also produced parts for tanks, gun mountings, aircraft components, parts for ships and complex secret devices which the technicians of the automobile industry were well trained to execute and bring into being.
Objections have been taken in this house relevant to the differential in automobile prices in the United States and Canada. I agree that at the present time there is a variance of about $450 in the price of the popular four-door model of the three most popular lower-priced cars. This does not take into consideration a slight reduction in price made recently by one of the manufacturers.
Let us see how this is made up, and I take my information from a publication of the Canadian automotive chamber of commerce. The factory list price in Canada of this model is $1,836; the factory list price in the United States is $1,609, which gives a differential of $227. There is a sales tax in Canada of $145 and as there is no sales tax in the United States that gives a further differential of $145. The excise tax in Canada is $217 as compared with $134 in the United States, which gives a differential of $83. The total sales and excise taxes are $228 greater in Canada than in the United States. Therefore the price to the Canadian consumer is $2,198, and to the United States consumer $1,743, or a differential of $455. With the permission of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I should like to place on Hansard a table giving the figures I have just quoted.

We have no desire of being merely the woodshed of the United States. Neither are we content to remain an agricultural community without a market for our farm products. It is essential that we have a well balanced economy in which the workman in the factory supplies the tools and equipment and the farmer on the land provides the food and raw products, but one in which both obtain a fair share of the profit.
Before there was any motorcar industry in Canada there was a customs duty of 35 per cent on automobiles. But there was no automobile industry to protect. The customs duty was and has been a source of revenue in Canada. Since United States manufacturers have seen fit to establish the industry in Canada, the customs duty has been reduced at various stages until it is now 17 J per cent on motor vehicles imported from the United States. The United States manufacturer is well able to supply the needs of the Canadian market at any or all times, but because of the tariff protection he finds that the motor vehicle can be manufactured in Canada using Canadian labour and a large percentage of Canadian material for less than what the motor vehicle would cost in the United States plus the duty to import it into Canada.
At the present time Canadian manufacturers import the frames for motor vehicles as well as the metal bodies. A few other minor parts are manufactured in the United States. On the other hand, there are many feeder plants in the Windsor area in particular which are manufacturing parts for American automobile manufacturers in job lots. Just a few days ago I had the pleasure of visiting one of these plants and there found that a great deal of their work comprised jobs for United States manufacturers which were rush orders.
The reason for importation of frames and metal bodies is that the equipment necessary for these parts is terrifically expensive and it is found that the parts can be imported and duty paid for an amount less than it would cost to build a piece of equipment to perform the operation. If a huge stamping machine or press is constructed to stamp out the metal body for a car at a cost of $200,000 -and I have no idea whether or not that is anywhere near correct as I have no connection with the automobile companies themselves-the cost of that press must be added to the price of the particular model sold. If
100,000	units are sold, $2 per unit of the sale price must be applied to the cost of the press.
iMr. Brown (Essex West).]

If 1,000 units are sold, for the purpose of my argument, then $200 of the sale price must be applied to the cost of the press or machine. This means that the selling price to the consumer of the individual unit must be considerably higher when there is smaller production.
Human nature being what it is, human tastes being fickle, and the needs of the purchasers being varied, there is not just one body model stamped out of the sheet metal. Each year the public and the public alone demands new and improved models which mean new dies and presses and increased expenditures resulting in higher prices to the consumer. This applies not only to metal bodies but to all parts of motor vehicles. The dies used in a punch press or stamping machine will make a thousand units or a million. If a million are made the cost of the die can be spread over the larger production. The same applies to component parts of a motor vehicle. An order far a million units will enable the feeder plant to cut its costs so that the unit can be supplied for less than the per unit cost of a small order.
The population of the United States is about 150 million people. In Canada we have only approximately 14 million. Production in the United States in 1952 was about thirteen times that of Canada. Therefore we can see that by reason of the greater population and higher demand orders will be much larger and costs will be correspondingly reduced. We are therefore paying an additional $227 per car for the privilege of buying a Canadian product, using Canadian labour and materials, and building up a balanced economy in the country.
In addition to the $227 for the privilege of buying Canadian, the consumer is paying an additional $228 approximately in hidden taxes which goes to pay for our national defence, family allowances, old age pensions, unemployment insurance, etc., for the benefit of all Canadians.
Remarks have been made at times that the automobile companies are making huge profits. Personally I do not represent any automobile company and have no stock in automobile companies, but I am vitally interested in the automobile industry because they are employers of labour in my community. I am sure that so long as there is a Liberal government they will be making money, and I like to see them make money because when they are making money the rest of the country is prosperous.
However, a few days ago I saw the annual statement of one of the larger companies

which showed that there had been a considerable profit; but when you stop to consider the amount of sales the profit amounted to something like 6 per cent of the sales made by the company last year. I do not think 6 per cent is considered to be an excess profit. I think you will find that the grocer considers that he has to make more than 6 per cent on his sales unless of course it is a huge supermarket. I think that the farmer considers he has to make more than 6 per cent, and I do not think anyone in this house or out of it will consider that a profit of 6 per cent on gross sales of any company or individual is excessive. That is what the profit was in this company. That does not take into consideration at all the amount invested as capital investment in the company but is merely the profit on sales.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is my view that the automobile industry is a vital part of the economy of the country, and as long as we provide a healthy atmosphere for business and commerce I am sure that the automobile industry will succeed and prosper and will give employment to individuals and small corporations throughout the whole country to the benefit of all.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Peace River has always been noted for his courtesy and co-operation and he deserves, I think, a special credit this morning as does the hon. member who has preceded me. I want to express my appreciation to them for having made way for me. Actually, the hon. member for Peace River should have spoken, but owing to an appointment which I have after lunch he agreed to let me speak now.
I do not wish to speak at any length in this debate but there are one or two matters which I wish to bring before the committee at this time. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has given us a very glowing picture of the trade of this nation and I do not think anyone can quarrel with the figures which he has presented. I would, however, like to direct to his attention one matter which is of particular importance. When the minister returned from his trip to South America some time ago he gave us a very glowing picture of the trip and of the possibilities which might flow from it. The minister can paint a glowing picture and gild the clouds, as we know, and he can also be most forthright and most direct-as he usually is. Some months have elapsed since he made that trip to South America and I would like the minister to deal specifically with it and to tell the committee this afternoon when he speaks just what concrete results he expects to flow from the trip. It is a matter of interest of course to all of Canada but particularly so to those of us in the east who are using maritime ports.

There was a time when we had extensive trade with Cuba and with the West Indies but our trade with South America has never been as satisfactory as we would like. There are undoubtedly possibilities for development there that the minister, with the research that he has done upon this, with the personal contacts he has established there, and with the emphasis which has been laid upon the possibility of the development of that market, should be in a position to speak upon concretely and directly to us. He might tell us what trade will flow or develop from his trip and from the publicity work which has gone into the development of that market.
The second matter I would like to draw to the minister's attention is one that I am sure he appreciates already. It concerns the proportion, the increasing proportion, of Canadian goods which are being directed for export through American ports. We have just listened to a graphic picture of the development of the automobile industry in this nation and of the importance that industry plays in our economic life. We all recognize that and appreciate it, and I think that Canadians generally are proud of the industry and are prepared to support it in any way possible as part of our integrated economic activity.
However, when one looks at the export figures one cannot help being alarmed at the increasing number of automobiles which are being produced in Canada for export and which are being exported through American ports rather than Canadian ports. I know that the minister can say that it is a matter for private enterprise and what can you do about it. It is true that it is a matter of private enterprise but private enterprise is very often influenced, and assisted, by national policy. The automobile industry is one of many private industries which have undoubtedly benefited by national policies inaugurated by this and preceding governments. I think that a government through its national policies can influence the development of private industry in more than one field and certainly this is one which is of tremendous importance to those of us in the east because although our exports are increasing and developing rapidly, the proportion of those exports going through American ports is increasing rather than decreasing. In the automobile industry it is particularly marked. When the minister speaks this afternoon I would like him to refer to that situation and tell us what if anything can be done to further the development of trade through Canadian ports. When I say "Canadian ports" I include all of them although the figures I refer to have application to the eastern American ports where trade has been diverted through government railways and other means to American ports.

Mr. Chairman, there is only one other matter to which I wish to refer and it is one that is of special importance to my own constituency. It has, of course, been mentioned before. It was mentioned last night by the hon. member for Eglinton, and other speakers have talked about it. Nevertheless it is a point which I want to stress formally, and that is the supreme importance of again getting access to the sterling markets and the markets of Great Britain. As all hon. member have said, it is a matter which is of importance to all of Canada: but there is no constituency in Canada, no area in Canada, which is more greatly affected than that which I have the honour to represent-the Annapolis valley with its fruit-producing industry. Not so many years ago the Annapolis valley produced and exported more apples to Great Britain than all of the rest of the empire and commonwealth together. As a matter of fact Great Britain imported more apples from the Annapolis valley than she did from all of the rest of the world- and that was just prior to the last war. Since then our exports have continued to go out the window for various reasons until last year we did not ship one single barrel or box of apples from Nova Scotia.

I am not familiar with the figures and all I know is that last year no apples went to Britain. course, there are economic developments in the industry. For instance, baby food-and to use a popular phrase, because I do not know the technical term-I suspect that manufacturers of Pablum and other baby foods are today in the market for thousands and tens of thousands of bushels of apples. A few years ago that market was not open to us. From time to time there will be crop failures in the United States and we will be able to ship apples there on those occasions- and we will be very thankful when those opportunities present themselves.
Everyone wants B.C. apples.

I am not going to enter into a discussion with you on that; but I am sure that if there were enough Nova Scotia apples for general consumption then those who were able to get them would not want British Columbia apples and they would hardly recognize them as such.
We ship them to Halifax.
Be careful.

I am not going to indulge in that discussion but I am more alarmed at the remark of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra than that of the hon. member for Fraser Valley.
What I am saying is that the American market, though in some ways it may be a substitute from time to time, is not a solution to our problem. That is obvious for two reasons. In the first place, as the minister knows better than anyone else, our trade balance with the United States today is such that we are in a most vulnerable position. Figures have been put on the record before and I am not going to deal with them now, but our imbalance of imports over exports is such that we are not in a satisfactory position. More than that, the Americans produce large quantities of good quality apples and when the crop years are right they themselves have a surplus. As the minister knows, they not only supply the local market but unfortunately they export and they receive a bonus for offshore trading which-even if we did get access to the export market-puts us in a difficult position.
The last time we sold apples in any quantity to Great Britain, the United States producers were getting a bonus of $1.25 per box on the export market, and we had to meet that in order to get into the market. We are prepared to do that. The industry in the valley has been revolutionized, owing in part to help from this government and in part to the energy which has been shown by the growers themselves. The industry has

been put in a position where, from a production standpoint, it will compete favourably with any apple industry in North America. But it does need the export market. Situated in Nova Scotia, on the periphery of this continent, the industry is to a large extent precluded from taking advantage of our own market. But by that very geographical position, jutting out as a sort of wharf into the Atlantic, we are enabled to take advantage of the British market. We can truck the apples to Halifax, put them on a boat and land them in the British market within a few days.
But something more must be done than has been done in that connection. I am not going to review what has been said before. We know the record of our demands that greater emphasis should be placed on the development of the British market. We have had resolution after resolution moved to that effect defeated by the government majority here because they have suggested that there was nothing that could be done. Now, we read in the United States papers, and I noticed in the New York Times the other day, that responsible writers are prognosticating movements which are taking place behind the scenes. It is alleged that there are discussions between the Canadian, United States and British governments, as well as the international settlement bank, as a result of which something is going to be done to bring about convertibility of currencies. I think that is possible, Mr. Chairman.
If such developments are taking place, then we should know about them now. The fruit industry is not one in which you can operate on short-term planning. The growers should know now what the possibilities are so that they can decide whether or not they can afford to spray, and whether or not they can afford to look after their crop. They could decide whether or not there is any possibility of a market for the crop. There is nothing which is more important to the people generally across Canada, and particularly in my own constituency, than the necessity of once more getting access to the British market. I hope when the minister speaks again this afternoon he will, if he can, deal frankly with this matter just as he usually deals frankly with these matters. If he can make any statement with respect to developments, I feel he should do so and give us the information now to enable the growers to make proper plans for this year's production.

I have been keenly interested in this whole matter of trade for quite a number of years, and although I have not spoken too often about it in the house yet
Supply-Trade and Commerce I have listened with great respect and interest to those things that have been said and the various policies and proposals put forward by means of which it was hoped to assist the world to get back into some sort of balanced economy. I feel that I should speak at this time to put forward once more the views which I have held for a good number of years, and also put before the minister a matter of great interest and concern to my own constituency.
First I should like, Mr. Chairman, to deal with trade generally and to trace, for just a moment or two, some of the facts about world trade which have contributed to the present impasse. For a number of years now, I shall not attempt to say the exact number, there has been what may be called a maladjustment in the world economy. This maladjustment has been of tremendous concern to most thinking people, and I imagine it has to the government. What I have observed thus far as a consequence of their concern has not impressed me as being action that would in any way tend to alleviate the serious condition. I think that if we had followed different policies from those which we have followed, particularly since the end of the war, or if one were to name a specific date, 1949, we could have prevented some very serious dislocations that have occurred in our own Canadian economy. I might refer, as one specific example, to this whole matter of the fruit marketing which the hon. member who has just finished speaking mentioned.
This maladjustment of the whole world trade and economy I think has shown itself more particularly in the relationship between the dollar and sterling areas. Since 1949 a number of discussions have been held amongst the various nations concerned, and attempts made to find some sort of makeshift, I shall call it, because that is all they seem to have been trying to do. They have been finding some sort of makeshift to enable the sterling area to carry on just a little bit longer without collapse. It seemed to me that there was nothing fundamental in their search or in their thinking; it has been somewhat superficial. Let us put crutches under the old thing they say, to hold it up a little longer so it will not completely fall on us.
So far as I am aware, no real effort has been made to get down to the real root of things with a view to finding a permanent solution to this very serious maladjustment. What happened, for example, at the recent Washington conference has been kept strictly secret. We do not know, therefore, what proposals were put forward. Certain things leaked out, I suppose, and became confused. The suggestion is that, out of the Washington

Supply-Trade and Commerce conference, there is going to come some successful solution to the inconvertibility of currencies. Well, Mr. Chairman, I think that we should have been given a whole lot more information than we have been given about the results of the Washington conference. We are in the dark, and as a consequence it is very difficult to discuss in an intelligent manner the problem that we now face with respect to world trade. I am convinced that nothing short of a fundamental change in outlook on the part of the nations concerned can produce a permanent remedy to the trade sickness which has so long afflicted the world.
_ Now, getting right down to basic considerations, I think it can be demonstrated that the United States has had a wrong outlook for quite a number of years towards this whole matter of trading. I am not attacking the United States at all when I say that. But when any nation with the industrial might of our good neighbour to the south has a wrong attitude toward this world economy, unbalance is bound to result. Then, when other nations like Canada voluntarily follow the United States in their wrong outlook, the unbalance of course is seriously aggravated; that has been the case in the past few years. Finally, when under political pressure the rest of the world is whipped into line by the United States, then it becomes next to impossible to restore the equilibrium in trade matters until that outlook is changed.
Now there is not the slightest doubt in my mind that the source of the world trade slump is the economic unbalance that has been brought about by such a policy on the part of the policy makers in the United States and Canada, and their inability to face the realities or to base their policies upon realistic thinking as to what would balance the economy from a world point of view. Now, what is a balanced economy? I say it would be one in which the production and exchange of different kinds of commodities and services corresponds very closely to human needs. Nothing less than that could possibly be called a balanced world economy. That is the only kind of world economy, in my judgment, that could flourish and expand steadily in the years ahead. Right now, this world does not have such a balance. I would say it is far from it, largely as a consequence of selfish shortsighted policies laid down and slavishly followed by, I will go so far as to say, adolescent human beings or, in the alternative, forced upon nations by powerful


financial and economic combinations of men. It should be perfectly obvious, I would think, to any grown-up, mature person that the only way to correct-in a permanent way, let us say-the present economic unbalance in the world is to restore the balance as quickly as possible. That is just ordinary, common horse sense. I realize that what I suggest is a big order, of course-how to correct the unbalance as quickly as possible-and I admit at once that it is much easier said than done. But it must be clear to anyone in this committee that it will not ever be done unless we deliberately and with determination set out to do it, and not just attempt to put crutches under an old arrangement which just cannot possibly stand by itself.
Over the years the United States has built up an ever-expanding balanced economy, balanced internally as well as externally, except when she refuses to recognize that the rest of the world cannot buy from her unless she is prepared to buy from them. She did so by protecting her own industry from external competition that might have been a destructive type of competition without that protection. She also built it up by attracting both skilled manpower and capital from Britain and other parts of the world in the early stages of her development. By the time world war I ended the United States had built up a tremendous surplus productive capacity and, as a consequence, the United States forced huge quantities of surplus goods into the channels of world trade without any effort to create an external balance either by increasing her imports or by consistent investment in other countries. Consequently by 1931 the unbalance had become so terrible that it erupted into the great depression that became world wide.
Faced with the necessity of trying to do something about it, as you will recall, the countries forming the British commonwealth of nations organized amongst themselves a preference system in order to present some sort of balancing factor in the world so as to offset the unbalance that was created by this huge United States industrial upsurge and the lack of world responsibility that was so evident within that country. This organization of a preference system amongst themselves helped the commonwealth nations tremendously and as a consequence they enjoyed a measure of balanced expansion for some years. But the nations of Europe which were prevented from helping each other to form an expanding, growing economy by the most-favoured-nation clause that was inserted in trade treaties were obliged to resort to every kind of restrictive device in order to save themselves. I speak there, of

course, of the unconditional most-favourednation clause in trade treaties.
World war II, I think, served only to aggravate the serious unbalance of the period between 1918 and 1939.	Then to make
matters worse, the United States threw all of its immense political and economic weight into what amounted to enforcement over the whole trade world of the very obstacles to recovery which had earlier been placed there; and she has been determined to prevent the building up of nation groups, with combined resources comparable to those of the United States, which would be capable, of course, of holding their own through a balanced, mutually expanding production and exchange among themselves, if necessary. The terms of the Washington loan, the Bretton Woods agreement, the Geneva agreement and the Havana charter have all been witnesses to the truth of that determination that I have spoken of on the part of the United States.
I am convinced that the only remedy for the present trade stalemate is the restoration of world balance by co-operation between relatively weak and unbalanced countries. They should be allowed to do that without any interference or restriction. As to whatever pledges the countries made under Bretton Woods, Geneva and GATT, anybody knows that they will inevitably and eventually be forced to evade them. The United States is evading them now. Other countries are forced to evade them. They cannot keep those terms and live up to their agreement, so they are being evaded wholesale today. The nations that are precluded from the free and flexible methods of co-operation by such things as mutual tariff preferences are having to resort to something else.
I am becoming much more impressed, Mr. Chairman, by the necessity for having the nations completely free to take whatever action they feel, in their own wisdom, they ought to take on the highest moral plane to bring balance and decency into this whole system of world trade. If they were allowed to build up mutual tariff preferences wherever it was found necessary, and freely adjusted currencies, I am sure they would not be driven by necessity to try to achieve something by such things as fixed import quotas, exchange controls and bilateral bargains that try to get in under the wire. Some of these things I have mentioned are damaging to their own enterprise and initiative as well as to world trade as well. I think the history of the nations in the last ten years would indicate that that statement is perfectly true. As I said, I am becoming a - great deal more impressed every day by the necessity for leaving the nations completely free to take whatever action they feel, in
Supply-Trade and Commerce their wisdom, they ought to take so that they can bring some sort of balance, decency and fairness into world trade.

Mr. Chairman, to continue what I had begun to say before lunch, in recent years Canada has drifted into the habit of buying from the United States, and at the same time trying to sell to Great Britain and to Europe, and then leaving it to others to complete the triangle of trade. This, of course, is exactly what the others cannot do under the present unbalance of trade.
Since 1949 Canada has found herself in the position that her natural and her best markets are increasingly restricting their purchases from Canada, except where they are paid for by the aid which these countries receive from the United States. Canada was the only commonwealth nation which, at Geneva, did seriously reduce her preferences on British imports.
I have often been led to ask our policy makers if they did not realize that by taking that action Canada was only adding to the difficulties that were faced by Great Britain in buying from Canada. We in Canada have drifted into a state of thinking that we are actually in the dollar area, although in our interests and our sympathies, as well as economically, we are linked a whole lot more closely with the British commonwealth and with Europe.
I wonder what would be the real difficulty in Canada's acknowledging that fact in the currency arrangements that she makes. Some time ago, when the Minister of Agriculture was in England he gave a speech in London in which he stated that some arrangements would have to be made by which Great Britain could buy her foodstuffs and other supplies in Canada, and that no currency restrictions ought to stand in the way of the successful achievement of that objective, and the achievement also of a balance in world trade. There is sense to what he said.
Undoubtedly the Minister of Agriculture realized that what I am saying now is true, that economically and in many other ways we are linked to Great Britain, the commonwealth and Europe more closely than with the United States, although in recent years we have got into the habit of thinking that we can tie ourselves to the United States and be safe. That is not true. I think we are finding it more so every month.
