I believe Canada should have started as far back as 1949 to accept payment in sterling for any balances owing us by Great Britain and by other parts of the sterling area. I realize all too well that it would probably have been necessary for us to accept sterling at a rate which we ourselves would find most convenient. I do not think there would have been any difficulty in arranging that, either.
I should point out, too, at this stage that the sterling area is a free association whose members can at any time change their rates to meet their requirements. If we had agreed to accept sterling, as I have suggested, and set a rate to suit our convenience, we could have shared with Great Britain a certain amount of protection against American competition, and at the same time we could have ensured that our people could enjoy satisfactory prices on the imports we bring into this country.
The only difficulty I can see about accepting sterling would have been this, that for the time being at least Canada would have found herself accumulating a surplus of sterling above our current requirements. These surpluses would, I suppose, have to be invested temporarily in the country owing the balance. But to offset that, there is every evidence that Canada has reached a stage of development where we could do that sort of thing safely, especially if we limited our commitments to a certain maximum figure until such time as the trade volume with the sterling area has come more nearly into balance.
Under such an arrangement, of course every sterling country, instead of restricting its purchases of Canadian goods, as those countries have been doing for the last few years, I think would go all-out to buy every pound of foodstuffs and other materials Canada could produce. I am satisfied European countries would have followed suit as far as they would find sterling an easier currency to meet than the American dollar. Instead of thinking about restricting the production of Canadian foodstuffs, as we have been thinking about it-and some of the farmers have been told they ought to do it- we could open up the valve and go all-out in production. There is a wider and perhaps much more important result than this that would have accrued from our willingness to accept sterling in payment for balances with Great Britain and the sterling area.
I think that such action would have gone far to strengthen the sterling area, and by now we probably would have begun to see some hope of achieving a balance in world trade.

I am convinced it would have been greatly to Canada's advantage if we had adopted the policy I have suggested as early as 1948, or certainly by 1949. I am also convinced that world balance in economy and trade can never be achieved under rigid agreements like Bretton Woods, Geneva or GATT. It can be achieved only if all the nations find themselves free to take whatever action they feel it is desirable to take, particularly along the lines of setting up and arranging mutually satisfactory co-operative associations, wherein they could present a united and comparable productive front to the great world industrial giant, the United States.
I should like to conclude this part of what I have to say about trade by pointing out the problem faced by the people in the United States today. To do this I should like to read briefly from the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of April 17, 1953, where, under the heading "U.S. Farm Problem", it says:
The United States government has $2,900,000,000 tied up in its farm price support program. As parity prices are guaranteed on principal farm products to the end of 1954, the government of that nation is somewhat in a quandary. The chief products involved are wheat, corn, tobacco and cotton.
Overseas markets for U.S. farm products are drying up. That is the main cause of the domestic problem. Farm exports in January were 29 per cent below a year ago. Cotton exports were down 63 per cent. Broader export markets are urgently needed, mainly by wheat and cotton growers. Higher import tariffs on the other hand are wanted by the dairy industry. This conflict puts the government under pressure. The administration would like an extension of the present trade agreement program allowing more time for study.
When you contemplate that situation, and also the situation that exists here in Canada, perhaps to a lesser degree at the moment but certainly growing, it becomes abundantly clear that we simply must find some means of distributing these surpluses. The suggestion that has been made of setting up a world pool or an international commodity clearing house organization for the distribution of surpluses seems to me the best that has been made thus far. We must find a way of distributing to the people who need them the surpluses that are bound to occur as we open the valves of our productive capacity and go all-out in peacetime production.
We are told that we had in Canada last fall something in the neighbourhood of 700,000 cases of salmon many of which are unsaleable at the moment. I am only quoting what a correspondent from British Columbia wrote recently to the Christian Science Monitor, as follows:
While the smaller salmon pack was not a matter of serious concern to packers who were faced with a carry-over of 700,000 unsold cases from 1951, fishermen have been hard hit. The market for

canned salmon has been restricted because of Britain's continued dollar shortage: Britain and the commonwealth countries having long been Canada's best customers for these exports.
The most recent figures indicate a present surplus stock of no less than 350,000 cases.
That seems to indicate a serious situation with respect to our ability to dispose of the salmon that we can gather in and put into cans. It just proves the seriousness of what I have mentioned. Now, I would like very briefly to deal with what I believe we can do in this country to make it easier for other people to buy our products. Two of the important factors in any cost of production are taxes and freight rates, over which this government has a very great influence and control. I believe that if this government could follow the suggestions of the opposition, namely to eliminate waste and extravagance and thereby reduce taxation, that would go a long way towards helping exporters reduce their prices. Also, if we could keep freight rates down, that would help materially in this regard.
A little earlier today the member for Moose Jaw brought up the question of our trade with Great Britain, and I would like to speak very briefly about that matter. The firm with which I am associated deals in textiles, and for the past thirty-five years, we have maintained a buying office in Manchester for the sole purpose of buying British textiles.
Since the war, we have not been able to buy a dollar's worth of textiles in the United Kingdom, and that has been due to three things. First of all, their patterns, which before the war were always attractive and very comparable with American and Canadian patterns, are now of an inferior nature, and, I am afraid, cannot compare with the textile patterns produced in this country and in the United States. Secondly, their prices are higher than the prices on this side of the water. Thirdly, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to get British manufacturers of textiles to promise or keep a delivery date. As anybody in business knows, it is vitally important to know when your goods are going to be shipped, and equally important to have them shipped at that time so that they may arrive in the country where they


are required for sale in time to be sampled for the trade before the selling season starts. If the goods do not arrive in time, they miss that year's market, and they are virtually worthless.
Our buyers have several times gone to Britain to try to revive the trade we did with Britain in those materials, but they have found the British very lackadaisical and in no way anxious to make promises of delivery; and we have found that a very discouraging factor when trying to do business with them.
I believe that every Canadian realizes the importance of buying all the goods we can possibly buy from Great Britain. I think, however, that the British people could do a great deal to help Canadians "buy British", and they could do it by bringing their designs to a level comparable with those available in the United States and Canada; by bringing their prices to a comparable level; and by realizing that it is vitally important, to those who sell their goods for them on this side of the water, to know when the goods will be shipped-and to have those shipment promises kept.
I think the British manufacturers could also do a great deal by improving their packaging methods, which I think are out of date as compared to those of Canada and the United States. I think they could also sell a great many more capital goods in this country by ensuring that those capital goods would be serviced once they were in use on this side of the water.
I know that for a few years after the war, British businessmen were hindered by a great many government restrictions, but to a large extent those restrictions have been removed in the last year or so, and I believe they can find no excuse on that score at the present time.
I believe that they should send out, as the member for Moose Jaw suggested, a great many more salesmen and representatives to sell their goods-and I mean really sell them in Canada-and also to find out from Canadian buyers what it is that they want so that those wants can be catered to in Britain in the production of goods for sale over here. I think also that they must realize that the United States merchandisers are very aggressive indeed. If British manufacturers are going to successfully compete against the goods we are buying from the United States at the present time, they must sell far more aggressively than they have done in the past. In short, and in conclusion, I would simply say to our friends in Great Britain that we in this country desperately want to buy far

more British goods than we buy at the present time, and I earnestly urge them to do a great deal more than they are doing now to help Canadians buy British.

The trade policy of this group, Mr. Chairman, was ably presented to the house by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I am not going to take the time of the house to deal further with it. I do want to bring a certain matter to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce at the request of the fruit growers in my constituency, as well as others who are interested in this question.
Last year the soft-fruit growers in the interior of British Columbia were very hard hit by a number of circumstances: the particularly large crop in the United States, the heavy crop in Canada, and then the change in the existing value of the dollar. They were able to sell only a percentage of their pack to the canners because the canners were well stocked and the demand for these products had lessened. I am speaking of canned peaches, canned apricots and soft fruits of that sort. The domestic market had already been considerably flooded by fresh soft fruit from the United States which matures somewhat earlier than ours.
This matter is one of increasing concern to the soft-fruit growers in the interior of British Columbia, to such an extent that it was the basis of a lengthy discussion at the annual convention of the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association held in January this year. I am going to read briefly two resolutions adopted by the convention and then bring this situation directly to the attention of the minister. In dealing with this question, the convention passed the following resolution:
Canned Fruit Import Controls
Whereas the orderly marketing of soft fruits is much dependent on cannery sales, and
Whereas the volume of imported canned peaches, pears and apricots in 1951 has reached four times the level of imports of these commodities for 1948, and
Whereas the volume of mixed fruit in can in 1951 has increased to 12 times the volume of 1948, and
Whereas there is no control of imports to Canada on these commodities;
Resolved that the council impress upon the proper government officials the seriousness of the tariff reductions accorded canned and processed imports in the current trade agreements, and press for every possible protection to the Canadian producer.
In addition I have received correspondence from various people. I will read briefly from one letter. I have in my hand a can of Australian peaches which are a sample of the peaches that are being sold in communities in my constituency, where the peach growers had to dump peaches last year, and where the 68108-2714
Supply-Trade and Commerce peach growers did not receive a sufficient return on their fruit to get back the cost of production. This is what my correspondent has to say:
These peaches are processed and exported by the Shepparton Fruit Preserving Company Limited of Shepparton, Victoria, Australia. They are imported by O. B. & Company of Vancouver, B.C. They come in heavy wooden cases. A case of 24 wholesale here at $9 and retail at 45 cents per tin. They do not compare in quality with our Okanagan peaches, being small and hard.
At Christmas time Australian Christmas cakes were also being sold throughout British Columbia that could just as well have been baked here.
If it were canned orange juice, oranges, or any of the many things that Australia produces that we do not, things that we need and can use and not interfere with our own home production, I think it would be a good move. But canned peaches and fruit cakes and such do not fall in this category.
Trusting you will bring this matter before the house and to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I do not know what the department can do in this connection. I am sure there are many products that we could import from Australia that do not compete with production in the district where the peaches are grown.
There is another aspect of this question, and that is that we are distinctly under the impression that these peaches are not nearly as high in quality as the peaches canned in British Columbia. They are canned under lower standards than ours and when I am finished speaking I shall send this tin over to the minister so that his officials can open it and compare the quality of the contents with the British Columbia canned fruit. The question of quality has also been given consideration by the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association. The convention passed another resolution which reads as follows: Peaches-Minimum Size
Resolved that this council recommend that the minimum size which peaches may be packed in Canada shall be two inches.
Marketing Survey
Whereas the distribution of fruits and vegetables is anything but satisfactory;
Resolved that this council request the division of economics, dominion Department of Agriculture, to make a survey of the entire marketing situation covering fruits and vegetables.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister, because I am quite sure his officials are interested in the growers problems. I should like them to consider the survey by the economics division of the Department of Agriculture, which has been suggested by the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association, and do all they can to see that we only get the things from Australia which we require and do not produce. It seems an absurdity- there are many absurdities under capitalism

Supply-Trade and Commerce -for peaches to come all the way from Australia and be sold in communities where the growers of peaches did not receive the cost of production last year. With those few words, I send the tin to the minister, for his inspection.

I rise primarily for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the members of the committee some words I wish to quote from the last issue of the London Economist commenting on Mr. Butler's budget of last week. The words I think are interesting, and if the minister -has not seen them I think he will be interested in them.
Sometimes the minister worries us a little by seeming almost too happy with the situation as it stands. Of course, after the moving tribute we have just heard from the member for Fort William, it is not perhaps surprising, but the rest of us will perhaps have to try and look at things in a somewhat more realistic fashion. We sometimes get worried because the minister so often is content, as he said the other day, to describe the present economic situation in Canada by saying that at no time in the past have Canadians been more prosperous. I am not going to dwell on tha-t except to reiterate what the member for Eglinton said, that if you tell that to the farmers who have lost their traditional markets in Britain for many of their products, they will not be very happy about it.
It is for that reason I want to say a word about the British market. I was troubled by what my colleague the member for Broadview said this afternoon, although I do realize that -those difficulties exist and that the British, perhaps in times -past, have been wanting in progressiveness. I am -hoping, partly because of what I -find in these pages of the Economist, that they may be pulling up their socks in that as in other ways. This year, of course, so far as trade is concerned, is a crucial year because of the fact that GATT is to be renewed-at least, we hope it is to be renewed, and the importance of our trade with Britain is of course accentuated greatly. The people in British Columbia can tell us a great deal about that.
-That leads me to the -point I wish to make. There has been a disposition over the decades, I suppose you might say over the generations, to write the old country off. I remember in the early years -of this century we were told that she was decadent economically, and the Germans were going to sweep everything before them; she really was a washout. Then, of course, we came to the first war when many people were ready to write -her off. The same thing occurred in the second war, and perhaps most of all in the years
[Mr. Herrldge.l

since -this last war, when we have been greatly troubled by the situation. It seemed perhaps that the traditional virtues of energy and initiative were being swallowed up or perhaps I should say tied -down by the mass of red tape and restrictions of all kinds. It is heartening to find that, as judged by the latest budget, they are emerging from that situation and that they are stepping out and are ready to take chances in the hope of returning to a world in which there will be freer and more profitable trade. With that comment, I wish to read a couple of extracts from the Economist of April 18, 1953-the one of a week ago-as follows, and I may say that this is to be found at page 130. Speaking of the budget it says- and these are Mr. Butler's words:
-"the reliefs which I shall propose are designed to improve our competitive efficiency, to provide incentives for greater effort, and to encourage private saving" or again "all reliefs are carefully designed for the prime purpose of giving the incentive for greater production."
Commenting on that the Economist says:
For the budget's greatest merit is one that cannot be put into figures. It marks a change of direction, a turning of the fiscal tide.
And again it says:
Whatever criticisms may be made of their details, they have the great recommendation that they mark a determination to "step out from the confines of restriction to the almost forgotten but beckoning prospects of freer endeavour and greater reward for effort."
I think that will warm the hearts of many of us and that we will wish them well in their effort which means so much to us as well as to them. I hope it will also stimulate us to make sure that we on this side of the water are doing every mortal thing we can. That leads me to mention one thing that has been mentioned before by others-and only yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton-and that is whether in fact we are trying in every possible way to make as many of our defence expenditures as possible across the water. The difficulties are great and the minister will no doubt do justice to that aspect of the matter. But on the other hand, as the old music hall catch said-and I have quoted it perhaps too often in this chamber before- where there is a will, there are three ways. I hope that much more can be done than has been done up to the present.

Mr. Chairman, as others have emphasized in this debate, I too want to say that the direction of our trade policies at the present time is such as to provide a real danger, particularly to the agricultural industry of this country. I believe that the United States market for agricultural products is in the main not a complementary one but a competitive one. The United States market is no

doubt the best market for Canadian pulp and minerals, but I believe that the loss we have sustained in the British market for many farm products has dealt and is dealing agriculture a serious blow. Unless steps are taken to recover the British market for many of these products, our agricultural industry is going to suffer. I say the United States market is not a reliable one for farm products. I think the Americans themselves have demonstrated that fact to us clearly in the restrictions they have placed on the importation of Canadian cheese, on Canadian dairy products and the suggested ban that might be placed on the importation of Canadian oats and feeds. Even as a market for Canadian cattle-and X see no alternative to that market-we can see the effects of competition from United States-produced cattle on the price of cattle in our own country.
Farmers were told last year by the Minister of Agriculture: "Keep your cattle home on the farm; you have nothing to worry about. Add another 300 or 400 pounds of weight to each head you have, and as soon as the United States embargo comes off you can ship your cattle into the United States and take advantage of the higher price." The minister had a floor price on cattle of $25 a hundredweight last year, and some of us thought that price was scarcely adequate. But when the floor went off and we were to get back into the United States market at the higher price, as the Minister of Agriculture had said, we find instead that cattle are selling much below the floor price that prevailed last fall. The United States cattle population is high and the Canadian cattle population is high. Economists tell us that for the next three or four years cattle producers can expect a further drop in the prices of cattle.
I think the British market is the only market in the world that can provide any hope for agricultural producers. Ever since I became a member of this house I have pointed out to the government the danger of losing the British market for Canadian products. Time and time again we in the C.C.F. have made the statement that we were losing the British market; and every time we said that, the government pooh-poohed the statement and said there was no foundation for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Is he aware of the fact that last year we shipped more food products,
Supply-Trade and Commerce both in volume and in value, than ever before in the peacetime history of this country?

As far as value goes, yes; but as far as volume goes, no. If I understand the way you arrive at your volume, you add it all up in pounds, in hundredweight; and of course the quantity of wheat adds up to a tremendous volume. But when compared to such products as cheese and bacon, the figure is of course not comparable at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Does the dollar value not matter?
I said as to dollars, yes, but as to volume, no; because I do not think you can compare 1,000 pounds of wheat to 1,000 pounds of cheese when you are adding up the quantities that we have shipped.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Why ship so much?
Why not let the hon. member make his speech?
The minister can make that point, but I say that the British balance of payments with Canada now is bad and the British are not likely to continue to buy that same high value of Canadian products.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, well-

I think that is the very reason Britain has not entered the international wheat agreement. I do not think it is a matter of another five cents a bushel one way or the other. Britain knows that her balance of payments position with Canada and with the United States is extremely adverse. I think that Britain is preparing to take drastic measures and that she has in mind a great deal more than just a nickel on a bushel of wheat. Let me tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce what his colleague the Minister of Agriculture has said in the past about Canada's trade position and the British market for agricultural products. The Minister of Agriculture is reported in the Regina Leader-Post to have said this at Qu'Appelle during the last general election. I quote from that article:
There is no evidence to support the contention of M. J. Coldwell, C.C.F. leader, that Canada is losing the British market for food-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Hear, hear.

It is true that the C.C.F. contended that Canada was losing the British market for food. I repeat that statement and I shall be able to prove it. Let us look at Canada's bacon shipments to Great Britain in 1946, after the war. They were 272-9 million pounds, valued at $61,400,000. Last year, shipments of Canadian bacon to Britain were zero. So there is no argument about
4290	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce whether the British market for Canadian bacon is going down or whether we are losing it. We have lost it; it is gone. Farmers of Canada believe that the British market for bacon we have had in the past was an important market.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Why do they not sell it at the British price, then?
And the government should take every possible step to see that that British market is opened.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is wide open in price.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce interrupts by asking what about price. Of course all that a government of the political complexion of the government in which the minister serves can think about is the matter of price. We in this group believe that if Canada can produce, and if our farmers do produce bacon that the people in Great Britain need, those people should have that bacon, and we should adopt whatever financial and trade measures are necessary to see that that bacon is moved to Great Britain, and to other European countries.
That is the trouble with the trade policy of this government: it is all price. And so by sending into the United States market our pulp and mineral products, Canada is prosperous. But when the government is going to supply any agricultural products to Great Britain it raises the old bogey of price.
Great Britain is short of Canadian dollars. We have lost the British market for farm products and agriculture does not face a recession-agriculture is in a recession right now, in commodities other than grain.
We have not done so well in the British market with our cheese. In 1946-and the figure I shall give is much less than the amount we shipped during the war-Canada shipped to Great Britain 92 million pounds of cheese valued at $18,420,000. Last year we shipped just 150,000 pounds of cheese valued at not eighteen and a half millions of dollars, not even one million dollars, but of a value of only $47,641. No wonder the cheese producers are not happy when their British market for cheese has now disappeared.
In 1946 we shipped 68 million dozen eggs to Great Britain valued at $25,500,000. Last year we shipped 2,374 pounds of dried eggs. Were they valued at $25,500,000?-not quite. Were they valued at $1 million?-not quite. They were valued at $2,700. And so, the British market for eggs is not being lost; it has disappeared.
We in the C.C.F. contend that unless Canada, in co-operation with other nations of the world, can reorganize international trade, in order to maintain and to increase our markets

in Great Britain for agricultural products, then the agricultural producers in this country face dire days ahead. This government has no vision when it comes to new and daring international trade policies. A few years ago the food and agriculture organization made great plans for an international commodity clearing house, a method by which countries producing exportable surpluses might get those surpluses to the nations in need of them. Under the plan the wealthier nations of the world would make financial arrangements to supply necessary currency to the commodity clearing house, and the countries that were to import agricultural products would obtain the currency from that organization in order to buy agricultural products throughout the world.
Well, our Minister of Agriculture went to that conference. He was against it. He was against the international commodity clearing house.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I never was against it.

Oh, yes, you were. The minister said, "We do not see any surplus of food in Canada. Even if there was, we feel we can deal with this through national policy." Well, we have had the minister and his national policy for some years, and we have seen the prices of agricultural commodities, one after another, go down, down, down.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Get my speech and read it.
The people of Great Britain, the people of Europe, the people of Asia-all those people need our food; and we have so much food in Canada that prices to agricultural producers are falling.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What I said in Rome was exactly the opposite of what you are saying.
Probably it is exactly the opposite, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Better read it.

-the Minister of Agriculture has always got an answer. And he always has an answer because every speech he makes is different from every other speech he has made; and he makes sure that he makes speeches on both sides of the question. Then if you try to nail him down he will say, "Look at the speech I made the month before"-or the month later, as the case may be.
Well, just a few days before the election in 1949 he said, "This C.C.F. contention that we are losing the British market for Canadian food is all wrong." I ask him today-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I did not say that, either.

for cheese? Where is the British market for eggs?
Well, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have a right to their own opinions. If they do not think that market is important, all right. But the agricultural producers and those who represent the people engaged in agriculture know that the British market is important to the welfare of the Canadian economy and of Canadian agriculture.
The government says: "Well, it is a matter of price." Oh, certainly, it is always a matter of price-always a matter of dollars, with this government. The Minister of Agriculture, as I said, makes speeches of all kinds; and there was a famous quotation in a speech he made in the house not many weeks ago, when he was telling us about the big barns in Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will make another next week.

Very likely, and you had better change that one, too. He told us about the big barns in Alberta and the big houses the farmers had out there. He said he talked to farmers who had told him that they had built those barns and houses on 5-cent pork. Well, there is about as much sense in that statement as in many other statements the Minister of Agriculture has made.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Ask your friends in the front seats about what they built those barns on.
Well, they did not build them on 5-cent pork.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They built them on less than that.

No; they were probably attempting to pay off the mortgage with 5-cent pork, and never managed to do it. But they certainly never built barns on 5-cent pork.
The British balance of payments position with Canada, in my opinion, is cause for concern. I do not say that Canada alone can deal with this problem; it is one that has to be dealt with by both Canada and Great Britain, and is something that requires a good deal of thought by international organizations such as the food and agriculture organization.
The government says it is a matter of price in everything-a matter of price in everything but defence; and then it is a matter of what the government says Canada needs. In connection with our desire for markets for agricultural products, I say the thinking of the government should be based upon our needs and world needs and not on price alone. And if the government brought that kind of thinking to bear on this problem we, as a
23, 1953
Supply-Trade and Commerce nation, would be spending more than one dollar on economic and technical assistance for every hundred dollars we now spend on armaments. I can think of nothing that would help Canada more or help the world more than for us to spend $200 or $300 million to help move our surplus of food to those people in the world who need it. If we did that, I think we would get a greater return for the money we spend by way of obtaining peace, than we shall get for the $2 billion we are now spending on national defence.
In 1950 Great Britain purchased from Canada $68 million more than we purchased from her; in 1951 Great Britain purchased $214 million more from us than we purchased from her; in 1952 Great Britain purchased from Canada $386 million more than we purchased from her. I think it is that $386 million adverse position in Britain's balance of payments with Canada that is now determining British policy toward buying our wheat.
Some steps have to be taken by Canada and some steps have to be taken by Great Britain to see that this large gap is narrowed. I hope that we will not leave it only to Great Britain, because if we do she will cut her purchases of wheat. She will do so until her payments position is balanced. I am fearful that she will be able to do so only by a further curtailment of purchases of Canadian commodities, particularly agricultural products, including wheat.
I have advocated the commodity clearing house which was proposed by the food and agriculture organization. I have pressed the need of moving our food to those countries of the world where people are hungry. I think the measures I have suggested and those suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) are sound, and that the government should follow our suggestions. In the meantime we are losing the British market. Instead of running the risk of further restrictions in British purchases of agricultural commodities and a further loss of that market, this government should adopt the policies I have suggested in order to regain the essential British market.

Mr. Chairman, I shall take but little time to say the few things I want to say in connection with the discussion that has gone on today and previously. I have listened to members of the opposition since last November complaining of the fact that we are doing such an enormous business with the United States of America. Why any sane-thinking person would criticize this government for seeking

Supply-Trade and Commerce all the markets that are possible in the Mr. Hees: Let us hear the Minister of United States I fail to understand.	Trade and Commerce say that.
Whoever did that?
Some hon. member says, "Whoever did that?" I have heard this remark made around this house one hundred times in this year: You should not put all your eggs in one basket.
Indicate the "some hon. member" who said that.
It was only five minutes ago that the hon. member sat down. He was suggesting more trade within NATO countries. Would he suggest free trade within NATO nations?
I am suggesting that we increase our trade with NATO nations.
Answer my question. If the hon. member is going to make a speech, let him sit down. I asked a question.
You asked me a question. I said we should increase our trade with all NATO nations.
The hon. member has not answered my question and I will ask him again: Do you support free trade within NATO nations?
I did not say that I supported free trade; I support increased trade.

The last time I spoke on this subject I suggested that there should be free trade within the NATO nations. If hon. members are honest and sincere in their desire to help the NATO nations they would be willing to adopt my suggestion and do away with tariff walls. I have never heard anyone in this group to my left suggest free trade among NATO nations.
Have you heard the cabinet suggest it?

I certainly have. If you will follow the procedure adopted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce during the four years since the last election you will find that he has used every method to try to bring about more liberal, and freer, trade with all countries.
Is this government a free trade government?
Absolutely.
Oh, oh.
Is it? Is it?
I tell you what I base that on.
Sit down.

I would like to ask the hon. member if he is prepared to go half-way in meeting any country. You cannot give it all away. I have just listened to the hon. member for Assiniboia talking about the markets that we have lost in Great Britain for Canadian products. Would the hon. member be willing to accept the prices that are being offered today by the British for the very things he mentioned? Is he prepared to accept those prices?
No.

That brings us back to the same old story. Only a month ago they were saying that taxation in this country was too high, that it was unbearable, but yet they are prepared to subsidize the producers of this country so that they may sell something that others do not want to buy. If that makes sense, I must be going the other way.
I think you are.

At least the hon. member knows where I stand; when I get up and speak on trade I mean what I say. Some of those I have listened to, I am sure in my opinion, do not mean just exactly what they say. I believe that everything we can sell in the United States today should be sold there.
On a point of order, no hon. member of the house should be allowed to say that another member did not mean what he said.
I said that that was my opinion.
You cannot express your opinion that way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Charlotte did not identify any hon. member. He said that he did not think some hon. members meant exactly what they said. I do not think he meant the hon. member for Eglinton.

On a point of order, I am sure that he did not mean me, because I have not been participating in this debate. The statement was directed at hon. members of this house and it was not a proper statement, being in breach of the rules of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. member will look at citation 299 of Beauchesne's second edition he will see that it is not in order for

an hon. member to say of another that he does not say what he means or does not mean what he says, but if the hon. member says that he does not think some hon. members say what they mean or mean what they say, that is a general statement without reference to anyone in particular.
I would like to remind hon. members, who perhaps on this occasion are particularly ticklish about expressions used by the hon. member for Charlotte, that I have heard expressions used which were much more offensive than this one and no one stood up and said that they should be withdrawn. I think the hon. member should be given some latitude and it should not be insisted that certain words be withdrawn on one occasion when on another occasion words which were perhaps much more offensive were not asked to be withdrawn. I do not think it is imperative that I ask the hon. member to withdraw the expression he has used as it was not made in reference to any hon. member in particular. At page 99 of Beauchesne's second edition we find this, for instance: That a member has taken a course unworthy of a minister.
And other expressions like that. I have heard such expressions in this house, and not very long ago either. Yesterday it was said that hon. members were taking directions from the minister the minute he stood up as to how they were to vote. Perhaps that was in contradiction of the ruling that was given not long ago having to do with accusing hon. members of not being independent. I think we ought to be reasonable about these expressions. The hon. member will remember that one time an hon. member asked that the word "irresponsible" be withdrawn. The hon. member himself claimed that the Speaker should not go that far, that after all some of these expressions had to be used sometimes. Let us not exaggerate.
I guess you had better be careful.

I will be careful. As I have said, there has been a great deal said here about our trading eggs, as you might call them, being all in one basket. There is another thing that makes me wonder in connection with that statement and that is whether it is better to sell to that market for cash or to give our commodities to somebody else. We all know that the British are keen traders. I admire them for that, but I believe that the prices they are quoting today would not be of a great deal of interest to the farmers of Canada. Surely it would not be right and proper to subsidize food and sell it in Britain when it can be sold for cash at a better price somewhere else. I do not believe 68108-272
Supply-Trade and Commerce that the people of Canada can be convinced that that is the right procedure to follow.
My friends to the left who seem to be disturbed can all remember that a few years ago the leader of their party was going to blast his way into the markets of the world. I watched that situation pretty carefully because at that time I found it pretty difficult to make a living myself. Many who sit here today may have found conditions during that particular period such that they could make a living without too much effort, but I worked longer hours than I ever worked before, harder than I ever worked before and made less than I have ever made in my lifetime.
See what a man it made of you, though.
So did everybody else.
I could not see that the explosives that had been suggested to get into these markets had been very helpful.
Everybody else in the world was doing the same thing.
No, they were not.
Sure they were.
I can tell the hon. member that I have heard members of his group stand up and speak in glowing terms about the great R. B. Bennett regime. They certainly do not remember what I remember.
You are talking about the great world-wide depression.
I remember it well. I remember conditions during the particular period when, as I have mentioned, they were going to blast their way into the markets of the world.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They blasted themselves out of office.

I heard the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, say some time afterwards that all the trade that was carried between Prince Edward Island and the mainland at that time could have been carried in a canoe. I agree with him there.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

If the hon. member will refer to page 3566 of Hansard of April 7 he will see how much more was shipped to Great Britain from 1930 to 1935 under the Conservative government than was shipped between 1936 and 1939.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I am glad the hon. member has brought up that question because if those goods -were shipped over there they must have all come from Ontario. None of them came from the maritimes. I lived down there and there was no great amount of goods going to Britain at that time. Therefore the central provinces must have taken full advantage of that.
We are talking about Canada. Get a broad view.
I suggest to the hon. member who interfered a few minutes ago that if he wants to take a broad view then we shall throw this thing wide open.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He was talking about shipping percentages.

I will tell you exactly why they are not doing it. There are people here on my left who could never accomplish it themselves, but they expect people from this country to go over to Britain and say: This is it, take it, no questions asked and no contradictions. That is what these people to my left are doing in the house. I do not believe they are sincere, but that is the kind of unreasonable statement they make with respect to trade. I believe the minister who conducts the affairs of this department has done everything that is humanly possible. We all realize the value of the British markets to this country. There is not a member in the house who does not realize that, but if we can sell to a market for cash then I do not want to see our products given away, and I do not believe the people of Canada want us to do that. I do not believe the people of Canada want us to subsidize if we can sell for cash. Am I right? You can go on and on saying that it should be done and that we should be helping these people. There are different plans today under which we are contributing enormous sums of money to countries which are not as well off as we are. There is the Colombo plan and there are other plans under which we are helping these countries. I support them in every way, but there is a limit to how much we can give away.
I am one who believes that as long as a cash market can be found we should not give away for nothing what has been produced by the sweat and toil of the people of Canada.
Who suggested giving it away?
The socialists.

The hon. member for Assiniboia who just spoke said that it should be done regardless of price. He said that he knew the Minister of Agriculture would ask whether he wanted to sell at the prices Britain was quoting, and he said that did not make a
LMr. Charlton.]

bit of difference. He said that price was no object, that it was just a matter of getting rid of it.
I believe that the way the trade of this country has been carried on since the war is a credit to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the officials of his department. I believe they are doing a swell job. I believe they are doing everything that it is humanly possible to do, and I do not believe that they have any right to tell Britain or any other country what it should do. I for one do not want to see that procedure followed. I believe that the British are in a position to run and control their own affairs in the way they want to deal with them.
I remember being over there in 1948 and being disturbed and worried because I found that Russian salmon was coming into Britain. There was not a single pound or dollar involved in the deal. The salmon was being bartered for tinplate. At that particular time we had plenty of salmon on the Pacific coast which could have been bartered for tinplate without any trouble at all, but Britain decided that it would take an inferior grade of salmon from Russia in exchange for tinplate in preference to the salmon in the warehouses in British Columbia. I do not say this in a critical sense, but may I add that during the war I could not buy a pound of salmon in this country. It was all given to Britain. I am not criticizing that because they needed it and I am glad they got it. We gave them all the salmon that we could produce, but when it came to paying for some on the line they bartered tinplate for Russian salmon of an inferior grade. I have one more word to say with respect to the criticism about trade with the United States.
Tell us about cigarettes.

I can tell you about cigarettes. We have a Minister of Finance who has been responsible this year for a reduction in the price of cigarettes to the extent of about six cents which I think was helpful to those who smoke cigarettes. But there is one thing that means a lot to the maritime provinces so far as the United States market is concerned. I refer to our pulp and paper business. Some people may say that there is nowhere else for them to get what they require, but let me suggest that if the United States market for pulp and paper was taken away from this country there would be a lot of unemployment in our pulp mills, logging camps and woodworking camps.
These markets mean so much to the maritime provinces and to every other province in the country that I cannot understand why anyone would suggest or think that we should

not take advantage of every market that we can get in the United States. It is our natural market.
Nobody is suggesting that we do not take advantage of every market in the United States.
If you are not, then a lot of idle talk has taken place here.
By whom?
A lot of idle talk has taken place since last November.
Quote names.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
What you are saying now is as idle as anything can be.
Mr. Chairman-

I rise on a point of order. I am addressing the Chair on a point of order. I have been trying to listen to the hon. member for Charlotte and have not had the opportunity to do so because of the heckling coming from the opposition. If the Conservative member for Broadview continues to heckle Liberal members like that he may expect the same thing in return when he speaks. It will be the golden rule. I have never seen anything like that. The hon. member who has the floor has been very patient, and I wonder that no member has risen before to protest against the continuous heckling of the hon. member for Broadview.
On a question of privilege, I get heckled just as much as the hon. member for Charlotte.
Did I heckle you?

I should like the hon. member to tell me where in my speech I intimated in any way that we should cut down trade with the United States. My remarks were quite to the contrary. I have suggested that we should do everything possible to increase our trade with the United States and all other countries.

I am pleased that I got up to make these few remarks because now there have been so many differences of opinion and contradictions that I will have to read Hansard to find out just where the hon. member stands. Before I resume my seat I want to emphasize the fact that I believe every effort has been made to increase trade with all countries. I believe that the trade mission from which the Minister of Trade and Commerce returned only a few weeks ago-

I know the people whom I represent do not want to produce unless there is a market for their produce and, in addition, they do not want the people of this country to subsidize produce or give it away to someone else. Let us take advantage of the markets open to us, and at the same time endeavour to increase markets in every other part of the world. To be sure, with these eggs that are all in one basket, let us protect the markets that we have. Let us not take chances on losing them, because when the time comes again to use a little dynamite or some other explosive to get them back we might meet the same result that we met between 1930 and 1935.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take two or three minutes of the time of the house on a matter which affects so many counties of western and southwestern Ontario; I refer to the growing of tobacco. Heretofore when I have spoken on tobacco in the house it was with the idea of having the duty or excise tax on cigarettes reduced in order to encourage increased production of tobacco, for the stabilization of the tobacco market generally, and to decrease smuggling. The hon. member who has just taken his seat in his speech a moment ago referred to the Minister of Finance as having only recently reduced the price of cigarettes by some 7 or 8 cents. That statement is probably as accurate as what he said about this government being a free trade government.

On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, what I said was that the Minister of Finance had been responsible for a reduction of 6 or 7 cents-a 5-cent reduction of his own and 2 cents which the manufacturers gave as a consequence of the minister's reduction. I did not say that he reduced them 7 per cent. Read Hansard tomorrow.

I do not have to read it; I have ears and I listen. The member said

Supply-Trade and Commerce just now that the minister was responsible for a decrease of 7 or 8 cents and that the minister's reduction was some 5 cents a package, but that was not the reduction at all. I wish he would look up the records and make himself a little more aware of the facts before he makes statements in the house which are wrong.
Hear, hear.

The same thing goes with respect to the tariffs applied by this government on goods leaving or entering the country.
For some fifty odd years we have been developing an industry in southwestern Ontario which has meant a great deal to our economy, although it has had its setbacks because of high taxes and high duties placed on certain of its products. It has been my privilege since I came to the house to advocate a different argument to that which I make today, because on previous occasions I suggested that the government consider reduction of the excise taxes and duties on cigarettes in order to encourage and support the industry. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that I have never heard any Liberal member representing a riding that grows tobacco advocate in this house a reduction of duties or excise taxes on any tobacco product

I rise on a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman. As I understood the hon. member he said that he had never heard a member on this side of the house rise in his place to protest against excise taxes on cigarettes. If he will refer to Hansard he may see what other Liberal members and I had to say last year; and credit for the decreases in excise taxes on tobacco is due as much or more to the Liberal party than to any other party in this house.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I must apologize to the hon. member if I am wrong, and I accept his statement because I cannot do otherwise and be fair to him. However, I wish to remind him that since 1945, when I came into the house, it has been a lonesome road over here in the matter of endeavouring to impress upon the government that it was its duty or responsibility to reduce the excise taxes and duties on tobacco products. If there was one lone voice from the government benches it was very faint. In all probability that voice was simply asking for a reduction in the taxes which have been put on by this government since it came into power. Never in the history of the country have taxes on tobacco products been as high as they have been under the Liberal government, and let there be no mistake about that.

My purpose in rising now is to express the hope that this industry can be encouraged. 1 think, with the number of trade commissioners we have in various leading trading nations in the world today, an opportunity is now presented to those representatives in those countries to develop markets for our various products, and I refer particularly to our tobacco. I am very happy to tell this house that we take second place to no one in the world in the types of tobacco we produce. In western Ontario and in the regions which go still farther north we grow the flue tobacco which goes into cigarettes. I am very glad to say that in that part of Ontario we also grow what is known as dark tobacco and burley tobacco. In the province of Quebec they continue to extend the growing of tobacco that is used in the fillers and the binders when making cigars.
I think the house will agree with me that the reduction of the duties on cigarettes is going to give an impetus to the tobacco industry generally. That will apply not only to growers but to manufacturers and, I hope, to wholesalers and retailers. I think the acreage which can be used for growing these different types of tobacco can be greatly increased, but what concerns most of the tobacco growers in Canada today is the price which they get for their product and the markets which they have.
Markets seem to be none too certain in any given year. Owing to exchange difficulties we find that our market for tobacco in Britain has been seriously curtailed, and in all probability that will reflect itself in the price which growers will receive for their product.
I mention this, Mr. Chairman, because the other day one of the members of my party was kind enough to draw to my attention an article in the publication Foreign Trade, dated April 18. On page 191 there is a reference to Portugal's imports of tobacco leaf for 1952 in the amount of $3,816,000, as compared with a slightly smaller amount for 1951. I think we are all seriously concerned with promoting the sales of the various commodities which we in this country can produce in abundance. What interested me, Mr. Chairman, was the fact that Portugal's imports came from the United States, Greece and the Portuguese overseas possessions. According to this report the United States shipped about three-quarters of the amount imported by Portugal.
I mention these tobacco imports because we in this country can produce very much the same type of tobacco that the United States produces. There is only one type of tobacco that the United States produces which we do not produce, and that is what is called a

tobacco binder. We do not grow that in this country. When it comes to cigarette or pipe tobacco we do not take second place to the United States as far as quality is concerned. I am very happy to be able to say that to the hon. members of this house. I hope that the minister and his officials will take cognizance of this situation and will endeavour, through the trade commissioners in these very important trading nations, to see that some effort is made to market quantities of our Canadian-grown tobacco. I do know there are certain countries which require different types of tobacco, but I feel satisfied that in this country we can grow tobacco that can be imported and used by all these trading nations for either cigarette or pipe tobacco.
I noticed with a good deal of pleasure, and I am sure this applies to other members of the house, a statement recently made by the minister in which he said that the number of countries in which trade commissioners were located had increased over a year ago. He stated that the younger people on the staff are being encouraged to take training to become more proficient for that purpose. I hope these trade commissioners will endeavour to get a toehold, so to speak, in these various countries. Even small exports would be appreciated, because I know if they do import some of our good tobacco it will mean increased sales as the years go by. Such sales would help to stabilize the market for the grower, because there would be so many more outlets for what he is able to produce.
The other important matter with which I shall deal very briefly is the sugar situation as we find it today in Canada. I have dealt with this subject at some length on two occasions, and upon the minister's return from South America he gave a review of what had taken place during his visit to Cuba. I appreciate that. Just recently an agreement has been reached between the processors in western Ontario and the sugar beet growers. The price no doubt will be determined to a great extent by the price of raw sugar which is, of course, set in New York, that being the world price. I believe the minister indicated that the representatives of the refining industry would go to Cuba and report to him on their return. Through a question placed on the order paper I have asked if any such report was made, and have been advised that a verbal report was expected within a short time. Thus far no report has been given to the house. In view of the fact that this situation is so critical, and the fact that so many people in western Ontario-in fact all the growers in Canada-are dependent upon this

Supply-Trade and Commerce price, I think we are entitled to some statement from the minister as to what the prospects are for the marketing of sugar beets this year.
Have steps been taken to curb the importation of Cuban sugar into Canada? When the minister spoke in the house after his trip he said there would be no refined sugar coming into the three western provinces or into the sugar beet area of western Ontario. I am not going to repeat what I have said before, nor do I apologize to anybody for what I did say. I was speaking on behalf of the sugar beet growers of this country, who today face peril and calamity with respect to the marketing of their products. There has been no assurance given by the minister or by anybody on behalf of the government as to what the prospects are for these growers. I am going to be brief in my remarks. I think people are entitled to a statement, because I am quite sure a report has been made to the department by these refinery representatives who were asked to go to Cuba.
If this were a matter involving only a few dollars it would not be so important. It is, however, a matter involving millions of dollars and thousands and thousands of growers. As I said before, if we crucify one segment of our primary producers today and another segment tomorrow, we will not have any left and we shall be dependent upon foreign sources for those requirements. I am going to say, too, that the minister was speaking in a little town in Perth county not long ago. I am sure he was aware that refined sugar had been coming into Canada, and certainly it was coming directly from Cuba. It was easy enough to find out how it was coming here. It was being shipped through New York in bond direct from Cuba.
In his speech in Mitchell-I have here only a monitored statement from CKNX, Wingham -the minister is reported as having said:
The sugar institute undertook to see that the members of the institute would not ship here, and so far as I can find out they have been successful so far.
This speech was made on March 29 of this year. I want to say to this house not a pound of sugar is shipped out of Cuba except under a certificate issued by the sugar institute. No independent processor can ship one pound of sugar out of Cuba without getting such a certificate. The co-operation we are getting from Cuba seems to me to be very doubtful, from the attitude I have seen expressed in the Cuban press as well as from the statement made by the minister upon his return from South America.

The people of Cuba are going to ship refined sugar into this country until this country takes the necessary steps to stop it. Thus far they have not taken those steps, that I can see. At the time the minister spoke in the town of Mitchell he was asked by the largest sugar beet grower in Canada, a young man by the name of Wilfred Brockman, who was very much interested in what the minister had to say, on this question -I am quoting now from a newspaper report, and it reads as follows:

Mr. Chairman, I think I can take care of myself. I want him to know that I have been interested in the sugar beet growers just the same as I have been interested in the tobacco growers in this country, because both those groups have surrounded me ever since I was born. That is nothing to apologize for.

I take an interest, of course, in the sugar beet growers of this country and the tobacco growers; and for that interest I make no apology to the minister, to this government or to anybody else in Canada. I have taken that interest during the time that I have been a member of this house; and as long as I am-and I expect to be here after the next election-I shall continue to do what I have been doing in the past. I think the minister may as well know that, as far as the sugar beet growers are concerned, a statement like that which he made in Mitchell does not reflect what I would call or what they would assume to be a fair practice, when he said in the House of Commons that there would be no refined sugar from Cuba going into the sugar beet growing areas of western Ontario and the three western provinces, and then qualifies it by saying that it will not come
