I know there were a few people here the other day from the various provinces of Canada-Manitoba, Alberta, Quebec and Ontario, I think- representing the sugar beet growers, who had a consultation with the minister. I want him to

Supply-Trade and Commerce tell the committee if any assurance was given them as to what they could expect, and if he by any chance indicated that there was some embargo on Cuban refined sugar. I was given to understand that statement was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the sugar beet growers had wanted my hon. friend's presence at that time I am sure they would have invited him. It happened to be a private conference, and I do not know that he is entitled to know what happened.

The sugar beet growers who came down here were certainly given some information that Would be of value to the sugar beet growers of this country, which the minister would have been able to give them. It may have been private so far as the minister and those representatives were concerned. But I think it is of vital public interest that matters of such concern should be made available to the public generally. Those people were after information they wanted to take back to the growers of their respective provinces. If some embargo is to be placed upon Cuban refined sugar for 30 days, then let the minister tell the house if that is so, and how it is being done. Let him also tell the house how he is going to stop the importation of refined sugar into any part of Canada, as he said when he spoke after his return from Cuba.
The sugar beet growers of these four provinces in Canada are entitled to a statement from the minister as to the government's intentions with respect to the preservation of their industry, which has meant so much to the economy of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the remarks already made by the hon. member for Kootenay West regarding the apple and soft fruit growers of Canada, and particularly those in British Columbia. I am not going to deal with all soft fruits although I could, because I have received numerous letters setting out the personal loss and inconvenience caused these growers by lack of markets and unfair competition. I have letters showing where the finest prunes that can be grown in Canada, or anywhere else on the North American continent, were sold for as low as 9 cents a crate. I have other letters showing where half a crop had to be dumped in the ravine to get it out of the way.
However, I should like to take this opportunity to deal particularly with the plight of the peach growers. A few days ago I received a letter from a man who has been growing peaches in the Okanagan valley for the last twelve years. In 1949 he picked 40 tons of peaches from his then young and promising


orchard. The severe frost of a few years ago killed a third of his trees and damaged almost all the balance of them, with the result that in 1950 he had no crop.
Incidentally those growers received compensation, but his total compensation for the loss of all those trees was only $38, to help him in replanting. This year his orchard recovered to the point where he had 20 tons of first-class peaches. The bulk were sold to the cannery. Some of them netted him $63 a ton and some $40 a ton, or an average of somewhere around $50 a ton. The choicest peaches of all were sold for an average of less than 50 cents a large crate. These were sold as fresh peaches on the domestic market.
The sad part of his story is that while the cost of production was almost $70 a ton, he sold them at an average price of $50. The growers of British Columbia I must say have not been idle in trying to remedy their marketing conditions. They have organized into one of the finest growers' organizations on the whole of the North American continent. But even so they can only see to it that they have a first-class product ready for market. The growers, naturally, look to the government for assistance in protecting the domestic market which, at the present time, could absorb all the peaches grown in Ontario and British Columbia combined, if it were not for what I consider unfair American competition, which last year amounted to approximately 12 million pounds of canned peaches alone. This dealt a severe blow to the Canadian canners, who now have a combined carryover of more than 25 million pounds of canned peaches.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the time has arrived when the government should take an interest in this problem. They have taken some responsibility for butter, eggs, pork products and wheat. I do not think that the fruit growers are asking, nor would they accept, charity; but they are asking the government to investigate the situation in connection with the importation of soft fruits from the United States.
I realize that much could be done on a provincial level. We in British Columbia have a soft fruits and vegetables market consuming roughly $5 million worth of those commodities annually. Yet $3 million worth of the products going to that market was supplied by the importation of fruits and vegetable from the United States. As I have pointed out before, this condition is general in every province; it is not confined to British Columbia.
I notice in The Grower, a publication issued by the Ontario fruit and vegetable association, some very pertinent facts in

respect of the marketing of peaches. They set out on an approximate basis the value of the total quantity of peaches sold. I shall not quote the figures, because I would not be in order if I were to do so, but I can say that the processors of peaches paid $2,125,000 in 1951 for 22,627 tons. The domestic fresh fruit market was probably greater than that. They estimate that for 1952 there would be a drop of 9,453 tons in the quantity to be processed. This was caused by the heavy carryover. On June 30, 1951, there was a carryover of 13,670,000 pounds of canned peaches. On June 30, 1952, a year later, there was a carryover of 25,355,000 pounds. Naturally this forced a reduction in the pack for 1952-53.
It is pointed out in The Grower that during 1951 Canadians imported 11,805,000 pounds of canned peaches from other countries, chiefly the United States, and exported only 57,000 pounds of our own canned product. The publication also points out the fact that from 1948 to 1951 inclusive the sale of imported fruit cocktails jumped from 2,079,971 pounds to 25,397,276 pounds. Estimating a third of the contents of fruit cocktails to consist of peaches, this would indicate another 10 million pounds of peaches imported in that form, or from 5,000 to 6,000 tons.
Without this tremendous and unbalanced importation, Canadian peach growers grew enough to supply the whole market. The Grower goes on to blame partly the antiquated processing methods used in Ontario. However, that does not apply to British Columbia, where we have a similar marketing problem. Our methods are quite up to date in our canneries.
The answer to this complaint could well be for the government to advance loans on a long-term basis at a low interest rate to cooperative processing plants, thus enabling them to bring down processing costs by the use of more modern machinery. I presume that price is a major factor in the sale of canned peaches. Through modern methods of production, methods which we should have with government help, the United States has been able to quote prices that have captured the Canadian market to the extent of 12,000,000 pounds after paying heavy transport costs and a duty of approximately $50 per ton on peaches. I hate to use the term "dumping", but I feel we have a serious situation there which to my mind amounts to dumping, and that is why I think it should be investigated. I realize also that high freight rates, along with the recent increases, will further handicap our growers.
As The Grower points out, surely there is something wrong when a nation of 15
Supply-Trade and Commerce million people are importing 12 million pounds of peaches, whereas a nation of 150 million will take in return only 57,000 pounds of our canned peaches. This problem involves government policy. We ask that a fair break be given the soft fruit growers, both in British Columbia and Ontario, by setting up an investigating body to see if something cannot be done to protect our own domestic markets for our own goods.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few questions I should like to ask the minister. I have in my hand the Canada Year Book for 1951, and on page 890 I see that in 1948, the year the present minister became head of the Department of Trade and Commerce, our total imports amounted to $2,636,945,000. In the same year our total exports amounted to $3,075,438,000. I would appreciate very much if I could have the total of Canadian exports and imports for 1935, when there was a change of government in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In 1935 the exports to all countries were $756,600,000 and imports from all countries were $522,400,000.
I thank the minister for that information. Could the minister tell us the total amount of Canadian imports and exports last year?
There were two wars in between.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In 1952 the total exports of Canada to all countries were $4,400,000,000 and the total imports were $4,050,000,000.

I thank the minister for the information. There has been a tremendous increase in imports from 1948, when they totalled $2,636,945,000 and when the minister took charge, to the total of $4,050,000,000 last year. In the case of exports the increase was from $3,075,438,000 to $4,400,000,000. These figures show that today our trade is much greater than it was in 1935 when the Liberal administration took office, and they indicate also the progress that has been made by the Department of Trade and Commerce under the present minister.
I am always satisfied with good results. I cannot argue with those who put the needs of their constituencies on the record, as that is their right; but as far as my electors are concerned I am perfectly satisfied with the good results that have been achieved by the Department of Trade and Commerce under the present minister.
The minister carries on many occupations with equal success, something which I cannot understand his being able to do. I think the success of the Department of Trade and

Supply-Trade and Commerce Commerce is due to his initiative and the constant assistance that is given to Canadian businessmen by the officials. I have had occasion to get in touch with the export and import branches of the department, and I was surprised to learn the amount of information that was at the disposal of Canadians who intended to trade with other countries.
I believe I have said this already in the house, but I want to take this opportunity to state again, that the international trade fair held at Toronto has put Canada on the map. It brings businessmen from many countries to Canada where they have an opportunity to meet Canadian businessmen. This fair, which was brought about through the initiative of the minister, has done a lot to promote Canadian trade.
Another action by the minister that has brought good results is the trip he made to South America. Some years ago a similar trip was made by his predecessor, and the results were quite good. But the last trip of the present minister to the various countries of Central and South America was the thing Canada needed to increase our trade with these friendly countries. I have some friends there who tell me that the minister was received not only as an ambassador of good will but as a prince by the chiefs of state of those countries.
What the Department of Trade and Commerce has done under the present minister is to make all facts accessible to all. There is a weekly periodical published by the Department of Trade and Commerce which is very useful. It has a fine appearance and it is the best kind of publicity for promoting our trade.
I know the minister is modest, and I find him very patient with some speeches that are made. I could say much more to praise the department which he leads, but for me it is not speeches that count. It is, as I said in the first place, results; and the results under the splendid leadership of the Minister of Trade and Commerce have been so good that everybody should be satisfied with the progress that Canada has made in trade.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Temiscouata is indeed a very special pleader in this matter, but it is rather unusual to me at least to feel that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to retain counsel to reply on his behalf. I believe he is quite capable of doing that himself, and why the hon. member felt that an explanation was in order, and why he had to put all the questions he did to the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a little hard for me to understand. But he does it in a very admirable way. I 

should think the information he gave was very useful, but he did not go quite far enough.
I am more interested in facts that in theories.

So am I, but I suggest to the hon. member that inasmuch as he was getting this information he might well have asked the minister the value of war production during the years from 1935 to 1952. That is very material.
It is on top of that. Everything has been good.
This is separate.
Although my hon. friend pictures it in black, it is pink.

No; a little grey, I would say. After all in the nighttime all cats are grey. But even after hearing these glowing figures I still have a little doubt in my mind when I hear hon. members from all parts of the country get up and talk about the market for peaches being bad, the market for apples being bad, the bacon situation being tough-I do not mean the bacon itself-tobacco sort of in trouble, cheese not very easy to sell, wheat also in a little difficult situation, lumber bad, base metals going down and mines closing. One begins to wonder what is going on. Of course we have to admit, even as the hon. member for Temiscouata will admit, that money is definitely going up in amount, but it is certainly very much less in value.
While there is no question that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is doing a good job, I wonder just how good that job really is, because we have several hon. members complaining about these markets and the difficulties of selling products. What is the answer? Is the answer that the Department of Trade and Commerce is not doing its job properly, or is it that the markets are not able to absorb the products? I am not competent to talk about the items I have enumerated, and possibly it may be considered that I am not even fully competent to discuss the question that I propose to discuss now. However, I notice that no members from the maritime provinces or from Newfoundland have mentioned the question of fish. The markets of those provinces at the present time, both for salt fish and fresh fish, are very definitely in the doldrums. The minister is fully aware of that.
With respect to the salt fish market, part of the minister's recent hegira to the West Indies and South America was the special visit he made to Brazil. I am told, although I may be wrong, that the special visit to Brazil was for one purpose only, to inquire

as to the market for salt fish. I understand that no good whatsoever came out of that visit in so far as opening the market is concerned. That is an extremely serious matter because in the old days, and not so old at that, Brazil was one of the greatest markets Newfoundland had, at one time buying something like 400,000 quintals of fish. That market is now closed, and of course with any market closed to Newfoundland salt codfish it puts an added burden on the markets to which the maritime provinces sell.
I am sure the minister will tell us that he has done everything possible with respect to the Brazilian market, but it is a very serious matter. If it were possible for that market to absorb 100,000 quintals of salt codfish, then the salt codfish situation would be eased as far as Newfoundland is concerned, and consequently that would ease other maritime markets. I presume the minister has tried every possible means to make that market available. I do not know whether it is a question of the Brazilian people not having the money or what the situation is, but even if it is necessary to lend them money that is so much better than to try to put a floor price under fish.
At the present time the fresh fish business is in a very bad condition indeed. There is a tremendous glut on the market, and Canada has not been getting her share of the increased purchases in the United States in the past few years. United States consumption has gone up but Canada, while still the largest supplier of fresh frozen fish to the United States, has practically remained in a stable position while the sales of the competitors of Canadian fish have gone up amazingly. I should like to give certain figures so that hon. members may understand the situation clearly. They appear in an editorial in the Daily News of Newfoundland of April 15. I am not going to read the editorial, but will merely quote the figures.
In the period from 1950 to 1952, while Canada's shipments of frozen cod fillets to the United States remained practically stable, Iceland's rose by 300 per cent and Norway's shipments by 500 per cent. That is an extraordinary situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What was the size of the shipments in 1950? Percentages are sometimes misleading.

I shall give the sizes, and they are by no means small. Canadian sales in 1950 amounted to 51,067,000 pounds and in 1952 they amounted to 54,807,000 pounds. In 1950 Iceland shipped only 12,529,000 pounds to the United States, but in 1952 its sales
Supply-Trade and Commerce rose to 35,487,000 pounds. That is not peanuts; that is fresh frozen fish. In 1950 Norway shipped 2,080,000 pounds and in 1952
10,540,000	pounds. In other words they had increases while Canada's market in the United States was stable. We did not sell any more, but those two countries increased their sales of fresh frozen fish by 31 million pounds over what they had been selling before. I do not blame the minister for it, but certainly somebody has very definitely missed out in this market.
It is easy to say that Iceland has been forced to sell more to the United States because of the loss of the British market. As the minister knows, the reason for that loss of the British market was the embargo placed on Icelandic fish by Britain as the result of Iceland extending her territorial water against Britain's wishes. I think that is the reason, though whatever the reason is it has set up this reaction now and we- and I mean the maritimes as well as Newfoundland-are finding the market for fresh frozen fish terribly sticky indeed. It may be a temporary matter and the minister may be able to evaluate these things much better than we can, but it is serious indeed.
When the hon. member for Lambton West was talking about his sugar beets and Cuba, I was thinking that it is not altogether an easy situation to handle. I hope he will not disagree with me too much, but while it is very nice to say that we will not buy any sugar from Cuba and that we will use our own, I am sure that the minister will agree with me-and I do not like to agree with him too much-that if we do not purchase sugar from Cuba they will not be able to purchase fish from us. Therefore I think there must be some kind of a happy medium in the matter. We have to approach the problem of trade carefully, and not completely shut off a market which we are dealing with. We have to approach it in the light of what they buy from us and what they want to sell to us.
We have sugar beets too.

I know you have, but this has to be worked out. We cannot suddenly put up the barriers and say that we are not going to do any business at all.
I have before me a clipping from the Daily News of April 15, 1953. It contains an Associated Press dispatch from Washington dated April 14 referring to a meeting to be called by North Atlantic fisheries interests and the United States. They proposed to put up tariffs on fresh frozen fillets; and I read:
Under present tariff schedules imports of frozen fish fillets are taxed 13 cents a pound on the first 15

Supply-Trade and Commerce per cent of domestic consumption or 15 million pounds, whichever is larger. Thereafter the duty is 24 cents a pound.
The new plan calls for a flat duty on all imports of 2J cents a pound.
That is only a report of the meeting so far and the matter has not gone to the United States congress. However, if the plan is presented and if the United States government adopts the recommendation, it is going to be practically ruinous for the frozen fish industry of Canada. I am sure the minister has had that in his mind when dealing with the question of fish, but if he has not had it there before I trust that he will remember it in future.
We also have the rather extraordinary spectacle that when our own frozen fish and salt fish trade is, as I said, in the doldrums Canada is importing a very large variety of fish, fish which we produce in Canada ourselves. According to an order of the house which was tabled on March 30, Canada bought $6,265,094 worth of fish in 1952. More than half, $3,280,000 worth of fish, was purchased from the United States. As an amateur in this trade and commerce business it does seem to me that it is a rather extraordinary situation that at a time when we cannot sell our own fish to the country we need to sell it to, we should be buying fish from that country. It may be that it is the sugar beet and Cuba question all over again; but it is something that I just do not undersand and cannot explain in any way. I trust that the minister will be able to give me a little light on it later.
The last matter I wish to refer to is the question of new industries in Newfoundland today. We have the unusual spectacle of Newfoundland being changed to a more or less machine age, and that is being done in a tremendous hurry. I am sure the minister must have full knowledge of what is being attempted by the provincial government of Newfoundland, and that he is in a position to assure us that all is well in those new industries. He is doubtless very close to one of them indeed, as he himself opened the machine plant last August. I was not present at that opening because we do not receive invitations to be present on such occasions, but I believe he promised that there would be extensive orders-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, are we going to continue these secondhand rumours which my hon. friend peddles in the house? To whom did I promise orders? I did not promise anything in the hearing of my hon. friend, I am sure.
I said I was not present at the opening of the plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Let us not discuss the promises I made.

The promises did appear in the newspapers. I do not have the references with me, but I recall them at the time and they have been constantly repeated since by columnists writing in Newfoundland papers.
I have been attempting to get an answer to a question which I put on the order paper on March 6, but I have received only a very equivocal reply. The minister could say "yes" or "no" or "go to heaven" about that industry, and then there would be no question about the position. There would be no question about secondhand evidence or misquotations, merely a straightforward answer about what is going to be done about that machine plant.
This is a time when Newfoundland has not too much money to invest, and a great deal of money has been invested in that industry by the Newfoundland government. I believe that in all the industries that are now in operation or attempting to be put in operation there is some $25 million on loan. Where the industries are being entirely operated by the government, some $10 million has been given not as a gift but as an advance. The minister must know what is going on. A lot of us are very doubtful of the very rosy promises made by the premier of Newfoundland as to the future, but the minister does know what is going on and I think it is time he made a statement on this matter to Canada as a whole.
This is not too much to ask in connection with a new province. The minister has been very gracious in his approach to the problems we have, and I may say that he has given us material assistance through his department in a great number of ways. He very clearly keeps his finger on the problems, and I think it is time that he should tell us whether all is well in the industrial program of that new province.
The minister has listened to quite a bit of advice in speeches today and I was proposing to ask him four or five questions, but perhaps he wishes to make his statement first.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I can make my statement first if you wish. There have been a good many questions asked and I can answer you now or later, just as you like.
The first question was raised by the hon. [DOT] member for Eglinton about the loss of our markets in the United Kingdom, with particular reference to markets for products such as salmon, cheese, apples, bacon, etc. Our exports to the United Kingdom in 1952 showed a substantial increase in

both value and volume over the previous year, and at $745 million they reached the highest figure in the past five years. The United Kingdom is making steady improvement financially, and will continue to provide a major market for Canadian exports.
The hon. member asked about the loss of markets for food products, and the future for the export of Canadian wheat in view of the failure of the United Kingdom to accede to the international wheat agreement. First of all with reference to food products, I might say that the value of the food products shipped to England in 1952 was an all-time high for any peacetime year. He said that we had lost the market for canned salmon. Britain recently announced the purchase of $4,250,000 worth of canned salmon from the country. This purchase goes a long way toward reducing our carryover of canned salmon as a result of the unusually large catch last year. In so far as cheese is concerned, the British purchased about 5-5 million pounds of cheese this year from us. This purchase cleaned up all the surplus available at the time.
Now, now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We had difficulty buying it for delivery. We could have sold more.

What are the holdings of
cheese today?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not know.
If you do not know what the holdings are today, how can you say there is no surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Do you know what the holdings are?
I certainly do.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What are they, then?

It is not up to me to
answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If you knew, why did you
ask me?

I just wondered if you
knew.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: However, these fictitious surpluses of my hon. friends are not so apparent when you come to buy them.
Mr. Chairman, they are not fictitious.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I might say that we were
charged with the obligation of buying the surplus of dried milk. Hon. members heard the Minister of Agriculture say that we made provision for buying 10 million pounds, and
23, 1953
Supply-Trade and Commerce we have been able to buy less than 5 million pounds to date.

You expect it to be given
to you.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are buying it.
But at pretty low prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If the surplus position were
as bad as my hon. friend represents in this house, I think a little more would have been delivered. In 1952 the British purchased
706,000	bushels of apples out of the 1951 crop valued at $1,581,000. We were told today that there was no surplus from the 1952 crop. I think anyone who comes from the apple country will confirm that statement. Apples sold, and sold at a good price.
I turn now to bacon. Canadian prices of bacon have ruled above the support price of 23 cents to January 1 of this year, and at the moment are about $3.50 above the support price. In order to sell bacon or other meat products in the United Kingdom market, Canadian farmers would have to meet the prices charged by suppliers in Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, Denmark and Holland. In the case of bacon this would be $30.32 per 100 pounds f.o.b. Denmark or Holland against the present Canadian price of $36 f.o.b. the Canadian seaboard.
In so far as beef is concerned, the spread would be even wider. Top quality New Zealand beef is costing the United Kingdom an average of 14-5 cents per pound f.o.b. New Zealand, and Argentine top quality beef is about 19 cents per pound against the present Canadian price of approximately 37 cents per pound for good quality at the seaboard. In 1952 we exported 238 million pounds of animals and animal products, in spite of the fact that we had foot-and-mouth disease plaguing us throughout most of that year.
Now, what is the future for the export of Canadian wheat? A good deal has been said about our great surplus of wheat. We have had three extraordinarily large crops of wheat, one on top of the other. Last year we had the largest crop in the history of Canada, and the equivalent of two average crops before that. Selling has not been the problem; it has been transportation. Transportation is still the problem. If we had more wheat available at seaboard, we would be able to sell more wheat. One of the most crippling things that has happened to the marketing of wheat has been the elevator strike at the west coast.
Hon. members gloat over the trade figures for February and March, which show a drop in exports. That drop in exports is exactly equivalent to the amount of money we
4306	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce would have received for the wheat we could not ship from Vancouver because of the elevator strike. I am sure we will be hearing about the decline in exports during the campaign throughout the country, but that is the explanation. We cannot ship the lost quantity of wheat through the eastern ports because the capacity to handle it is not there. We hope to catch up by the end of the year, because we hope the strike is not going to last much longer.
I do not think hon. members wish me to discuss the wheat agreement situation, because a debate on that subject will occur some time next week when we discuss the resolution now on the order paper. I might say that whether or not the United Kingdom accedes to the agreement, she will still be buying wheat in Canada, as she has in the past.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Lethbridge really wants me to discuss GATT, or whether we can sit down quietly and discuss it between ourselves. He asked who started this idea. I think it was a spontaneous demand from all countries emerging from the war to lower the trade barriers. Canada was active in it. Mr. Wilgress was the first chairman at Geneva, and also chairman at Torquay. Every country took an interest in it. As a result of the general agreement on tariffs, we allowed in a great number of items duty free or at a reduced rate and we were protected against discriminatory tariffs on the part of other countries. I am sure the splendid increase in Canadian exports is due in no small measure to negotiations carried out under the aegis of GATT.
What are the prospects for convertibility of the pound? All I can say is that, as a result of a series of conferences in which Canada has taken part, all the countries who are interested in convertibility of the pound are working towards convertibility. The strengthening of the financial position of Britain is a step in the right direction. Conversations have been had by that country with Canada and with the United States concerning the measures that would be needed to place convertibility of the pound on a sound basis. Conversations are now taking place between the United Kingdom and the countries of Europe who would also require to work along the same lines, and all I can say is that steady progress is being made toward convertibility. I can say that anything Canada needs to do as her share towards bringing that about will be done.
Someone said that Canadian imports from the United Kingdom were being hampered by duties. I should like to point out that


of the total imports from the United Kingdom in 1951 worth $421 million, 59 per cent came in free of duty. Of the 41 per cent remaining, a good deal was represented by Scotch whisky, which carries a high rate of duty. Excluding the Scotch whisky, the average duty on the balance of the imports was charged at 5 per cent ad valorem. Therefore I think we can discard the theory that Canadian tariffs against United Kingdom goods are a factor in preventing the balance of trade.
The difficulty is that Canada has had a very rapidly expanding economy since the war. The requirements for imported goods have gone up faster than has the productivity of the United Kingdom. We do all we can to favour United Kingdom goods in this market. I think the United Kingdom is making progress in opening up markets here, particularly for manufactured goods which Britain is best able to sell and for which we provide one of the largest import markets in the world. I could give a number of examples of extremely successful efforts by British firms to export to this market in increasing quantities and to establish a market here for their goods, but I do not know that I need to take the time to do so at the moment.
It has been suggested that we are not doing all we can-

Their delivery rates are
better?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
They are getting a bit better, yes. The situation has been difficult. It has been a matter of lack of availability in the first place and a lack of reliable delivery dates. That situation is being corrected. British prices are in line, and I think the market in Canada for manufactured goods from Britain will grow as Britain becomes more firmly established with a representation in this country. This country imports currently about $600 million worth of equipment alone which Britain might well manufacture. Of that market Britain should take an increasing share.
The suggestion has been made that we should purchase war materials in Britain. The Department of Defence Production must purchase the type of equipment that the army orders, but we have placed substantial orders in the United Kingdom. I think to date the orders placed there amount to something in the order of $100 million. All of our heavy tanks are being purchased there, a certain amount of ammunition, the aircraft carrier, quite a number of airplanes including 15 for Trans-Canada Air Lines and two Comets for the R.C.A.F. It is the policy of

the Department of Defence Production to examine all requisitions from the army in order to determine whether they could be filled in England. If the material must be imported, the preference is given to the British market in filling the order.
We were asked what was going to happen with regard to Japan. The question was as to how we propose to meet Japanese competition in the Canadian market. In 1952 our sales to Japan were valued at $102 million and the imports from Japan at $13 million. Negotiations are proceeding for a trade agreement between Japan and Canada in an amicable and friendly manner, and we have good reason to believe that an agreement will be arrived at which will safeguard the interests of Canadian manufacturers and at the same time be mutually beneficial to both countries.
The leader of the C.C.F. party pointed out that participation of the United Kingdom in this market has gone down. During the depression the United Kingdom supplied us with up to 24 per cent of Canadian requirements; that is, exports from the United Kingdom to Canada were 24 per cent of Canadian requirements. But since 1945 the United Kingdom share has steadily decreased. The reason for that is, of course, that our requirements have grown much more rapidly than has the ability of the United Kingdom to produce for this market. There are many easier markets in the world for the United Kingdom to sell in. They can sell in India, Australia, and Egypt, which are traditional United Kingdom markets and which are also expanding rapidly and making a heavy demand on United Kingdom products. However, our exports to the United Kingdom have been growing from year to year; and while our imports have been holding about steady, we expect that situation will improve in their favour.
Then the leader of the C.C.F. party sug-j gested that we sell apples, salmon, cheese,\ bacon and other surplus products to the United Kingdom for sterling. We do sell for sterling, but we sell for convertible sterling,^ What I presume he means is that we sell * for inconvertible sterling. Inconvertible sterling is merely an agreement to pay dollars at some indefinite date in the future; it is a loan without interest and without a due date. Britain has never asked us to make that kind of loan. I suppose if Britain asked us to make almost any kind of loan we would consider it carefully; but I cannot for the life of me see why members of the House of Commons would urge that we make a
23, 1953
Supply-Trade and Commerce loan to Britain in the form of an interest-free advance with no due date, rather than an ordinary loan normally made between two countries. Inconvertible sterling is simply a promise to pay-in small denominations, probably-that we take and put in a safe; but that sort of transaction is not one that either the government of the United Kingdom or the government of Canada would favour. It is wholly impracticable. I do not see why that suggestion has persisted so long.
I think I have fairly well covered the points I wish to make. The hon. member for Annapolis-Kings asked for specific results from our Latin American trip. It is very difficult to give a list of direct sales made, except for the sale of 115,000 tons of wheat to Brazil, which sale was arranged at the time we were in Brazil. Every member of the mission did business, and has had further inquiries since his return to Canada. The Canadian exporters' association reports that more of its members have visited Latin America since our mission than at any other time. One of our leading paper mills reports the best business they have ever had in areas visited by their salesmen, and attributes this fact to the visit of our good will mission. Our farm implement manufacturers have had inquiries, and old customers have again asked for newsprint from Canada.
I think any other information required can be brought out on the various estimates.
Is there any possibility of giving me an answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend worries about the exports of fish. So far as I know, since Newfoundland joined the confederation her fish have been sold every year. I do not know of any fish that have remained unsold over the years. There is a surplus there now, but nothing that either Newfoundland or ourselves consider to be burdensome. We will continue to sell Newfoundland fish just as we have sold it ever since Newfoundland became part of Canada.
Does the minister consider the fish market is just about normal at the present time? Do you think the fish situation is about normal there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, I am not expressing any opinion. I cannot speak about every commodity in every part of Canada and say whether the market is normal or abnormal. But I say that since it has been our responsibility to sell Newfoundland fish, we have sold it all. We have found markets for it, and I express confidence that we will continue to do so.

I am not talking about Newfoundland only; I am talking about maritime fish as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, let us talk about the area you know, and not extend the discussion to areas you do not know much about.
What about the Brazilian market?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend has not had the Brazilian market since he can remember. There was a little fish put into Brazil on a barter deal a few years ago, fish for paper. Aside from that Newfoundland has been excluded from the Brazilian market for many years.
Is there any market in Brazil now?

When?
