The minister dealt with several matters about which I proposed to ask questions. However, there are two or three more I would bring to his attention. Would he tell the committee what results have followed by way of increased trade between Canada and the commonwealth countries as a result of the commonwealth economic conference which took place last November? I ask about that because it appears to me that the conference merely worked out a broad approach to the question of how trade generally could be increased. However, it may be that additional steps have been taken which have increased trade. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The economic conference in London was not a trade conference. No ministers of trade were there. It was a financial conference, attended by prime ministers and their ministers of finance. We sold more to the commonwealth countries last year than ever before in our history. It was the first time in history that our sales to the commonwealth exceeded a billion dollars. But I would not say that the economic conference was the particular cause of that situation.

Will there be any sort of trade conference at the gathering to take place after the coronation? I understand the senior ministers of the different commonwealth nations are to confer at that time. Will their discussions include commonwealth trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have not seen the agenda. Trade, of course, is always a subject matter for discussion; but it would not be what I would call a conference on trade.

Then will the minister give consideration to taking some definite steps to promote trade between Canada, and Australia and New Zealand? These countries would benefit from any commonwealth arrangement. However, as I understand the figures, our trade with those two nations is very low at this time, a matter that is of great concern to those of us on the west coast. I have here a copy of Foreign Trade for February 21, 1953 in which are listed the eleven leading countries in Canada's trade, for the years 1951 and 1952. In both those years Australia was ninth. As a matter of fact in 1952 the exports from Australia were $1 million more than in 1951, or a total of $50 million as against $49 million in the preceding year.
At one time Australia was our third best customer. Now she has dropped to the ninth position in exports, and she is eleventh in respect of imports to Canada. The trade figures show that in 1951 goods to a value of $45 million were imported by Canada from Australia, and that in 1952 goods to a value of only $20 million, or less than half, were imported.
Then at one time New Zealand was our eighth best customer. Now she is not even on the list. I do not know how far the figures for New Zealand are below those for Australia. However, Australia is ninth in her purchases from us and eleventh in our purchases from her. At one time Australia was our third best customer for lumber, following the United Kingdom and the United States in that respect. At times I believe South Africa bought more than was bought by Australia. Also, we formerly sold a great deal of canned salmon to both Australia and New Zealand. We now have
350,000	cases left in our warehouses, even after allowing for recent sales to the United Kingdom, and it is my understanding that no canned salmon is being sold either to Australia or New Zealand at the present time.
It seems to me that if the Department of Trade and Commerce put on a drive of the kind made to develop trade with South America, and if that were put on by the minister himself, there might be great benefit for Canada, Australia and New Zealand. This may not be the best way to approach the matter, but in my opinion there is a very serious problem involved. Something should be done to increase that trade.

We have on the west coast a new shipping line planning a service to Australia and New Zealand, but doing so I believe on a tentative basis. If trade cannot be increased I am afraid there is not much prospect of retaining a proper shipping service to Australia and New Zealand. Of course we can get there by plane within a few hours; they are no longer weeks away from the west coast of Canada.
We do feel greatly concerned however about the fact that trade between Canada and those two nations of the commonwealth has decreased so materially. Would the minister tell us whether anything can be done about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Trade with Australia and New Zealand is still a sterling area problem, just the same as our trade with the West Indies or with other sterling countries. At the conference held in January, 1952 all the dominions and colonies were asked to tighten up on their expenditures of American and Canadian dollars. They did so. They all imposed drastic prohibitions. Australia and New Zealand stopped importations of automobiles from Canada. That is only one item. I could add that they cut down on their importations of lumber and newsprint. Quotas were put on a large number of products. That accounts for the failure to sell canned salmon. All I can say is that the only hope of restoring the trade is to restore the financial position of the sterling countries to a point where they can afford to spend more dollars in Canada.

Were there not somewhat
similar obstacles in connection with promoting trade in South America?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, no.
Were there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Nothing to do with the sterling problem.

But there were exchange
problems and restrictions?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In certain countries, the Argentine and Brazil, there are restrictions. You mentioned Newfoundland codfish. The currency situation in Brazil has closed off that market for the time being. Argentina has prohibitions on many articles. As we come northward countries like Mexico, Colombia, Venezuela, Cuba, Haiti and the Dominican Republic, have practically no currency regulations. Their markets are just as free as the Canadian market.

Would the minister give some consideration to sending a mission to Australia and New Zealand. I believe that if
Supply-Trade and Commerce we sent representatives on a high level there might be a possibility of doing something about this trade situation. Another result would be to promote understanding among these three countries of the commonwealth.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would be delighted to head a mission to Australia and New Zealand. I would like to go there.
It would be a good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Anything that can be done in Australia and New Zealand can better be done through negotiation with their representatives in London. London is the banker of those countries. I am quite sure that no radical change in money quotas or money restrictions could be arranged anywhere except in London.

In his speech on April 17 the minister said that the general agreement on tariffs and trade would run out at the end of the present year. Presumably it is to be renegotiated. I took it from his remarks that Canada is in favour of the renegotiation of the agreement. Could the minister give us further details of government policy with regard to GATT and also with regard to the British preference?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Canada has no intention of changing its policy on either. We will certainly use our best efforts to see that GATT is extended for another three years. We have always maintained the British preference and always will, at least in the foreseeable future.
The Canadian government then has no intention of asking for a change in the British preference?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.
That is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We never have asked for it.

I am not so sure. My interpretation of what has happened in the past is not the same as the minister's. However I am talking about the policy at the present time with regard to the British preference and I understand from the minister that Canada is not going to ask for any change.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

I should like to have the minister's views with regard to the exportation of iron ore from the west coast to Japan. This has been discussed on previous occasions and, as he knows, I have suggested that the government should take some action to stop or at least reduce this export for fear that if it is continued it will delay or make impossible the establishment of a steel industry on the west coast.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
One answer the minister gave last year was that the exports of iron ore to Japan were made in small quantities and would not affect the situation. Our trouble is that our iron ore deposits are comparatively small; we have nothing like the huge deposits in Quebec and Labrador. I got figures today from the bureau of statistics which show that in the last calendar year 802,311 tons were exported to Japan from the west coast. The exports during the last half of the calendar year were far heavier than during the first half, being at a rate which would mean total exports for a full year of 1,103,232 tons.
This iron ore is dug from crown-granted claims, so the provincial government cannot impose restrictions on its export. It is dug out by a company owned in the United States, and shipped in Japanese bottoms. Canada gets about $7 per ton for this ore, yet we buy back from Japan steel which has a value of $150 and $200 per ton.
The great worry is that if this operation is carried on indefinitely there will not be enough iron ore on the coast to justify the establishment of a steel mill, or that the establishment of such a steel mill will be delayed. I would be grateful if the minister would give his views on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the iron ore situation in British Columbia is purely a matter for the provincial government. The government of British Columbia owns its natural resources; it owns this iron ore. If it has given mining rights to anyone the permit must have been given with the expectation that the ore would be exported because there is no present demand for it locally. I am certain that the province has the power to stop the mining of this ore any time it pleases.
I cannot think what the federal government could do about it. The federal government must make laws that apply all across Canada. The federal government would be most reluctant to stop the export of iron ore, because this phase of the industry is just beginning. We have been net importers of iron ore for a great many years, and we hope in a year or two to be net exporters. I would hate to do anything that would prevent the export of iron ore. If we did, Newfoundland would be affected because they have been supplying Britain with iron ore for many years and no doubt would like to continue to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The provisions of that act
require that certain conditions must obtain as a reason for interfering with exports. I am afraid the only way we could do it would be to use the Emergency Powers Act, and after the lashing we took on that for the past two days I would think-

I am not suggesting that for
one moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the only power on the statute books that would permit us to interfere with the situation.

I do not agree with that. I
submit that it could be done under the Export and Import Permits Act.

Mr. Chairman, before proceeding to ask the minister certain questions I should like to comment upon the report of the department. I think it is most regrettable that when we are studying the estimates of this department the report of the department is not available. I am indebted to the deputy minister of trade and commerce for sending me galley proofs of the report this morning. The minister tabled galley proofs in the house this morning, but of course they have not been made available to hon. members. This department is unlike some others in that its year is the calendar year and not the government fiscal year. That explains to some extent the delay in the tabling of the report for the year 1952, but I should like to say that I think it is highly important that in future the report of the department for the previous calendar year should be presented to the house in ample time before the estimates of the department are brought on for consideration in committee of supply, so that all members will have an opportunity of familiarizing

themselves with the contents of the report. It is an important report of an important department. I think a knowledge of the contents will not only help to expedite the work of the committee of supply, but it will also mean that members will be informed as they ought to be.
The first matter I should like to take up relates to the prime ministers' conference held in London last December. The minister has emphasized the fact that the conference was concerned with financial questions and not with trade. I think we are all aware of that fact. The report of the prime ministers' conference was, it seems to me, unfortunately vague and general in its terms. It may be that the deliberations of the conference were of such a nature as not to admit of a report being written in more specific terms. Nevertheless it is exceedingly vague and general.
I should like to take up a point with respect to the report of the prime ministers' conference in relation to the subject of convertibility, on which the minister made some comnjents. He indicated the importance which the government attaches, and I think rightly so, to convertibility as related to the trading outlook of the country. He did say that the government are prepared to take whatever measures they are asked to take to assist in bringing about convertibility.
I should like to ask the minister to develop that theme further and indicate what measures, if any, the Canadian government has been asked to take in that direction; what other measures, if any, are under consideration, and what answer has been given in relation to any particular request for measures that the Canadian government has been asked to take in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, I was not present at the conference. I have only read such report as was issued, and so far as I know no request has come up to this time for the Canadian government to take action. Convertibility is some distance away. I could not say whether it is a matter of months or years, but progress is being made in that direction. It is the intention to work toward convertibility at the earliest practical time, and I am certain that before final steps are taken requests will be made of Canada. All I can say is that Canada is very much interested in bringing about convertibility and will endeavour to do what is necessary at the time.

On the subject of our trade with the United Kingdom, the minister used the expression this afternoon that "we do all we can to favour United Kingdom goods in
Supply-Trade and Commerce our import markets." What did he refer to specifically there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Our trade commissioner service is at the service of anyone attempting to sell British goods here. If we are buying for the government abroad, we try to buy in the British market in preference to any other, in our own self-interest. I made the remark this afternoon, I think, that we bought from the United Kingdom something over $100 million worth of goods in the last year in munitions or in aircraft for T.C.A. and things of that kind. In other words, our desire is to buy in the United Kingdom in preference to any other market. It is not always possible; in fact it is only occasionally possible, but when it is possible that is our policy.

That was the point, Mr. Chairman. The minister made a statement with respect to government policy in relation to trade generally. It was at a later stage in his remarks that he took up the point of placing defence orders in the United Kingdom. But are we to understand that it is a definite policy and a matter of instruction on the part of the department to its officers who are placing orders, whether defence orders or otherwise, that where the goods cannot be furnished in the home market they should give a definite preference to the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would say so, price and quality being equal.
Oh yes, quite.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: And availability reasonably good. Sometimes we do not have the time to get the goods from the United Kingdom. Delivery is important, but if delivery, price and quality are equal we will favour the United Kingdom.

I think this is an appropriate point to ask the minister for clarification of an incident that created some degree of mystification at the time. About August 15 last the minister made a statement as reported in the press to the effect that Britain might receive $150 million worth of free armament from Canada this year. The press dispatch that came from London, following the appearance of a report to that effect in the Canadian press, indicated that at least some of the treasury spokesmen at London found it hard to understand the statement. They pointed out that if it was something new they did not understand it, and if it was a reference to something that had been undertaken before then it had been announced under circumstances that made it difficult to understand.
4312	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Would the minister make a full statement so we may have ample clarification of this matter? The dispatch I have before me is a Canadian Press dispatch from London dated August 15 which refers to another dispatch and reads in part as follows:
The dispatch said the program announced by Howe had been drawn up "at least six months ago. Canada herself is making no direct arms gift to the United Kingdom", the correspondent wrote. He added, that Canada's attitude has been described in Ottawa as "willingness to give Britain all help short of aid.'' Meantime in the British press there has been little other interpretative comment on the arms-gift arrangement.
Will the minister make a full clarifying statement now with regard to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think that would be more appropriate when we are discussing the estimates of defence production. It had to do with Sabre planes, which have been delivered steadily, and certain other goods. I do not remember the particulars at the moment. I was not prepared to discuss the matter on these estimates.

If the minister would prefer that I bring it up on the estimates of the other department I would be quite agreeable.
I thought it followed along naturally after our discussion on policy with reference to purchases from the United Kingdom, but I shall be glad to bring it up on the estimates of the other department.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, the last subject relating to our trade with the United Kingdom on which I should like to ask the minister for some further statement relates to the token import scheme that has been in effect and applied by the government of the United Kingdom since 1946. That you will recall, Mr. Chairman, is designed on the one hand to limit importations into the United Kingdom and at the same time permit certain commodities from abroad to be kept before the consuming public there. I mentioned last night that while the original quota set was 40 per cent of pre-war sales in the basic period 1936 to 1939, nevertheless effective January, 1952 that 40 per cent quota was cut to 30 per cent.
Imports into the United Kingdom under the terms of this scheme may not bulk large in total. The total in 1952 was $5,600,000 as compared with $7,500,000 in 1951. We are told in publications of the department in the last two years that the British purchase tax and competition from other countries have


made sales under the scheme more difficult. In the past year about 266 firms participated as against only 118 in 1946 when the scheme was first introduced.
I should ask the minister for some comment on the scheme and particularly whether the Canadian government has made any representations to the government of the United Kingdom with a view to liberalizing-if I may use that word with a small "1"

the provisions of the token import scheme, increasing the percentage or enlarging the scope within which Canadian exporters may operate under the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the token import scheme is still in effect applying to 30 per cent of pre-war exports, as my hon. friend has outlined. The quotas have not all been taken up, but I think about $5 million of them have. been. The scheme has been broadened and, of course, we are always bringing pressure on the British government to relax import controls to the greatest extent possible.
A few days ago I had a personal letter from the chancellor of the exchequer which outlined the present position. It is that there are world open licences which allow anyone to import certain commodities from any country in the world without any restriction as to quantity. They cover: nickel ores and concentrates, residues and matte; asbestos, raw and fibre; platinum ores and concentrates; cobalt metal (unwrought) and cobalt oxide; pig iron, iron ore; steel scrap.
Then there are open individual licences. These are in general issued to individual importers who apply for them. The holders may import unlimited quantities of the commodities covered so long as the open individual licence remains unrevoked. They normally involve an obligation to make regular returns of actual imports and future commitments, and they can be revoked if imports prove to be excessive. In the case of the commodities listed, the open individual licences apply to imports from any country in the world. The commodities are: wheat and flour on reversion to private trade; coarse grains on reversion to the private trade; softwood; lead; zinc.
Then there are specific licences. These are issued on application to individual importers, and allow the holder to import up to a value stated on the licence. Licences are normally issued on proof of essentiality, but in some cases they are issued by reference to a predetermined ceiling of total imports. In the case of some commodities, licences are issued on a non-discriminatory basis-that is the licence enables the holder to import from any non-sterling source. In the case of the other commodities the licence will generally

apply only to imports from the dollar area. In most cases non-dollar imports are licensed on a more liberal basis, generally under open general licences or individual licences which do not cover imports from dollar sources. The specific licences cover: bladders and casings; animal fats; linseed and linseed oil; beans for canning; tobacco; veneers; plywood; hardwood; pulp; newsprint; fertilizers; chemicals; kraft paper; abrasives; ferro alloys; steel; synthetic rubber; seeds and pitwood.
The government also makes direct purchases of:	cheese, rationed types; meat;
canned salmon; aluminum; oils and fats; copper, tungsten ores and concentrates.
That is the position today. The token import market scheme has been broadened to the extent I have indicated.
Do I understand that the commodities listed by the minister have been lifted entirely out of the scope of the token import restrictions?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. The licences are broader than those in the token import scheme. Generally speaking, the limitation is much less than in the token import scheme.

That is not too easy to follow. Are we to understand that the commodities which the minister has read in all cases lie outside the token import scheme and, as to such restrictions as do apply, those restrictions have been now lifted?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, to the extent I have indicated.
Is there any indication that the percentage for the past 15 months, the 30 per cent applicable under the token import scheme, is going to be raised in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, there is no indication of that. The import licence scheme is a holding operation to allow exporters of pre-war days to hold their brand name on the market. As financial conditions permit, the government of the United Kingdom is gradually moving out of that plan into a much broader plan to the extent that I have indicated, that is on the commodities I have named. There is no import licence required for a number of items; that is, they can be imported from anywhere in the world regardless of currency. Then there are other items that are subject to fixed quantities with no discrimination as to country. All this list is on a much broader basis than you are claiming.

I have a number of other matters to raise. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that it will be the wish of the house that the government should do all in its power
Supply-Trade and Commerce to encourage the removal of these restrictions by the British government. It is evident in the world today that quota restrictions and exchange restrictions, of this and other kinds, are more restrictive of trade than conventional tariffs. To the extent that the government will do all in its power to encourage the removal of these restrictions which have hampered the export of Canadian goods to the United Kingdom market, I am sure its efforts will be supported.
I should like to turn to several inquiries with relation to the United States. The minister made a brief reference this afternoon to GATT, and expressed the hope that it would be possible before the end of this year to carry forward an extension of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. I believe that view is shared by most of the members of this house. Will the minister tell the house what, if anything, the government has done in the way of feeling out the opinion of the United States government in this matter by opening negotiations. It is quite evident that the success of GATT in relation to its extension will depend very largely upon the attitude of the United States government.
President Eisenhower, in his inaugural speech, declared himself in favour of the extension of GATT, but he did not specify whether he meant simply an extension in point of time or an extension with respect to the commodities and rates covered by the present agreement. There have been various opinions expressed by members of the United States congress on their attitude towards GATT and that type of trade agreement. Will the minister tell us what, if anything, the Canadian government has done by way of opening negotiations with the United States administration on this subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The negotiations to which the hon. member refers will take place this autumn. Our officials are in close touch with the officials of the United States. Depending upon whether or not the powers of the reciprocal trade agreements act extend the president's power to make further concessions, we would look for an extension of time. If the reciprocal trade agreements act is extended, there may also be a widening of scope. After three rounds of tariff negotiations, the scope of GATT is about as wide as it can go at the present time. We would be glad to see it wider, but we are not too unhappy about it now.

I take it, then, from the minister's statement that the government really has not much hope that the extension

Supply-Trade and Commerce will apply to more commodities or carry the present agreements to a higher degree.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: 1 did not say that at all. I hope the hon. member is not going to suggest that I expressed an opinion on what the United States will do, because I cannot do that. I have not the faintest idea.

I asked the minister how we were to interpret his remark about the extension. We were talking about two kinds of extension, one an extension in point of time and the other an extension of the application of the general scheme of GATT.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, if the president's powers are allowed to expire we can then look for an extension of time. If his powers are renewed, then we can look for an extension in both time and scope; that is all I can say.

I wonder if the minister would say what the present position of Japan is in so far as GATT is concerned. Have they asked to come in? If they have, who is holding them out? Perhaps the minister would say what the attitude of the Canadian government is toward that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Japan has applied for admission to GATT. The application is under consideration. I do not know who is causing the delay; I suppose a number of people. As to what Canada's position is, I am not sure at the moment. In any case, it would not be important. The position of Japan will be considered, I am sure, at the next meeting of GATT, when a further decision will be made.

I should like to point out to the minister what I know he already knows. Japan is a country of over 85 million people. It has been stripped of the possessions it had before the war. It seems to me that if the Japanese are to live, they must export. I think it would be desirable, therefore, if they were brought into GATT. If they cannot trade with us I think they will have to turn to the communist countries. Therefore I hope the Canadian government will support their entrance to GATT when the time comes.
Will the minister tell us what efforts the Canadian government is making in the direction of customs simplification on the part of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There again, customs simplification on the part of the United States is a matter for the United States government. We are pressing for the United States to ratify that measure. The joint chamber of commerce of the United States and Canada has considered that particular problem, and have


been advocating it for some time. What is required now is congressional action.
We have been talking about the difficulties of this matter for many years. Has there been a real liberalization, say in the last four or five years, in the administrative policy of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There has been no change in the act in the last three or four years. There has been a more favourable approach to customs simplification. A bill has been drawn, and it is before the United States congress. I resent very much being asked any opinion of what the United States congress will do or what United States officials will do.
I was not asking the minister for any opinion on what the United States will do. I was asking about a matter of fact, and he has partially told me.

This afternoon the minister told me his department had a special import branch. I wonder if he would mind clarifying that statement a little. Will he say who is the head of the branch, what exactly are its duties, and what results it has had in encouraging imports in recent years?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The branch has been in existence for six or seven years. It is headed by a man named Charles McGinnis. The duties of the branch are to assist foreign exporters to find markets in this country for their goods. It has been very effective. The branch is the particular guardian of the trade commissioners from other countries, and it helps them carry out their duties in finding markets for the products of their countries in Canada. Similarly we have an export division which performs the same function for our exporters.
Would the minister care to say whether this particular branch has done any work in trying to encourage imports from Britain in the last year or two?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would not ask silly questions.
As long as the minister will answer them, it is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Will the hon. member admit that Britain is a country desiring to export to Canada?
I would think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Then this branch is functioning.
It may be a silly question, but I have never heard of this import branch which the minister says is active.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member has not been in Ottawa very long.
Has the branch just died a natural death or is it doing something to try to get our import figures up?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is not a committee. It never was a committee. I hate to teach my hon. friend the A, B, C's of government organization, but I may tell him that this is division A of the Department of Trade and Commerce. If he will look in the Department of Trade and Commerce annual report he will get the complete personnel, their salaries and their pedigrees. It has been in existence for a long time. If he will just read the departmental report he will not have to ask that question.

I am not particularly
interested in the pedigrees. All I should like to know-and I do not think the minister needs to get in a dither about it-is what they are doing to increase our British imports, if anything. If they are not doing anything, all he has to do is to say so. If they are doing anything, then let him tell us what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They are just doing that. They are working to try to increase British imports and to find a larger market for British goods, just as they are working for French goods, Italian goods, Australian goods and New Zealand goods; I could go through the whole list of 48 countries. They are working for all of them, trying to find markets for their products in Canada, and doing what they can to help to balance trade between Canada and all the countries with which she trades.
I want to ask a silly question.
That is not surprising.

I should like to know a little bit about the relationship between the export branch and our trade commissioners. For instance, if a Canadian manufacturer wants assistance, does he move through officials there and then does he go on to the trade commissioner, or does he establish direct contact with our trade commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is optional. He usually establishes direct contact. But if he wishes to go to our export division to find out what commodities a certain country can absorb, he will get advice there and then he will be directed to the trade commissioner service and be in touch with the trade commissioner directly.

This country and city were favoured a fortnight ago with a visit by the premier of France and several of the leading ministers of the French cabinet. Are negotiations being carried on between the Canadian and French governments with a view to a
Supply-Trade and Commerce new trade agreement within the scheme or the framework of GATT or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There are no trade agreements with countries that are members of GATT. GATT is a multilateral trade agreement in which all countries are placed on the same basis. There are no trade agreements with any country in the world that is a member of GATT.

Let us not quibble about terms. We know what the scheme of GATT is. All I asked was whether any negotiations are being carried on between Canada and France with reference to trade, or looking toward closer trade relations, or agreements of any kind with respect to trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; nothing of that kind. There could be no agreement. Trade arrangements are fixed for all countries that are members of GATT. They are all the same. We have a committee on trade with France-a committee of civil servants-which meets from time to time to study trade problems, to advise France of any trade opportunities here and to obtain their advice as to any opportunities for Canadian goods in France; but it is not a committee that makes trade agreements.

There are two other matters about which I should like to question the minister. The first is one I mentioned in my remarks last night. It concerns a press report which appeared on November 18, from which I read just the opening paragraphs. It is a Canadian Press dispatch and reads in part as follows:
The Canadian government has adopted a get-tough policy against alleged dumping of manufactured goods in Canada by two communist-dominated countries-Czechoslovakia and Poland.
Customs officials have been empowered to increase the value for duty on an imported item by as much as 50 per cent before applying the regular tariff charge. Thus the government will collect the duty plus the difference between the quoted and increased price.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The article is correct. It is impossible to get fair market values in either Czechoslovakia or Poland. We have asked for the information and we have not been able to get it. Therefore we apply fixed values for duty purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Fifty per cent is the limit fixed in the act.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Have you applied the maximum in all cases, or just in some?

speechtext: I do not know that. It has nothing to do with me. The Minister of National Revenue operates that machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in trade relations it is customary for foreign countries to allow officials of the government, particularly of the Department of National Revenue which has to do with the handling of customs and excise, in their countries where they may obtain values with reference to goods that are exported to Canada. I am sure hon. members are acquainted with the general principle, namely that the goods are invoiced into this country at a fair market value; that is at the prices at which they sell in the country of origin.
With reference to Czechoslovakia, the government carried on negotiations with its representatives in this country at that time, and asked for the privilege of having our representatives go into Czechoslovakia to obtain those values; and that privilege was denied. When it was denied, in order to give a fair share of protection to our own manufacturers with whom these exporters would be in competition, it was decided to apply the dumping duty. That dumping duty is a maximum of 50 per cent in advance of the prices at which those goods are invoiced into this country. That was applied on this occasion, and it was applied because of the fact that manufacturers in our own country, principally of textiles, complained to the government that textiles were being put on the Canadian market at prices less than the equivalent prices at which they were sold in the country of origin.

428.	Trade commissioner service, $2,522,696.

What is the difference between ambassadors, consuls, trade commissioners, honorary commercial agents and foreign service officers? We find all these under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and apparently all are doing the same work. That is, as I understand it, they are endeavouring to sell our goods in foreign countries. However, they all seem to be designated by different titles. For instance, in Buenos Aires

we have an ambassador, a consul and all the other officers. If a man wishes to make a deal with that country, should he go to a foreign service officer or to an honorary commercial agent, or to whom should he go? Perhaps he should go directly to the ambassador, if we have one there.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
An ambassador is the representative of the government in a country. He reports to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He is the diplomatic head of the Canadian mission in the country to which he is accredited. The consul is also an officer of the Department of External Affairs, and deals with various commercial documents on behalf of that department. A trade commissioner is a representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce, accredited to a country that does not have a diplomatic mission. He may be the senior representative of Canada in that country. For instance, in Haiti and the Dominican Republic we have trade commissioners as senior officers.
Then a commercial counsellor is a representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce who is attached to an embassy. That is, where an- ambassador is the representative of Canada in a country, he will have on his staff a commercial counsellor who is the equivalent of a trade commissioner in countries where there are no ambassadors.
Then in countries where we have no other representation, as in Bermuda, we have a local man who is known as an honorary commercial agent. In Bermuda he happens to be the head of Butterfields bank and, without cost to Canada, he is good enough to reply to our correspondence. If we have problems there we write to him, and he will straighten out the matters for us.

When the minister spoke on Friday evening he very properly informed us about the activities of this part of our service, which I feel is a very important one. Perhaps we have underestimated the value of the service this branch has given to our country. A trade commissioner in my opinion is really an ambassador of good will to another country. I feel that in selecting these men great care should be taken, because the position calls for special gifts and special qualifications. I do not think an ordinary college education alone qualifies a person to fill these positions properly. They require men of experience, men who are enthusiastic in the interests of Canada and who are willing if necessary to spend 24 hours a day to promote good will between Canada and the countries in which they are 68108-273

Supply-Trade and Commerce located. I hope careful consideration is being given to the selection of the people who will represent us.
Were any new trade offices opened in other countries during the last year, and is there any possibility of opening more in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member has mentioned favourably the trade commissioner service, because I believe it is a service that returns its cost to Canada many times over. I am really amazed by the accomplishments of some of our trade commissioners, in fact by nearly all of them. Every few days something turns up that shows extraordinary activity on the part of our trade commissioners, business coming to Canada that we would have lost had it not been for their activities.
Speaking on Friday night I said there were 48 offices with a staff of 379 including local staff. Within the last year we have opened three new offices, at Beirut, the Dominican Republic and New Orleans.
To what extent do these trade commissioners use films and radio in their work in these various countries, to advertise Canadian goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Each trade office has a projector, and they are supplied with a library of films. If there is any particular commercial film required by the office, they will write to the department in Ottawa. We try to rotate commercial film, and sometimes cultural film, so that eventually they travel to all the offices.

Is it the government's policy to encourage young Canadians to serve as typists, filing clerks and the like in these various offices in foreign countries? In my view that should be encouraged so these young people may be trained to take part in our extraterritorial service.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: When the factor of security is important we send people from Canada to fill the positions of stenographers and clerks. Where that is not necessary we try to employ Canadians who are resident in the area or, if that is not possible, we employ local residents who are not Canadians. However, I have visited most of the offices in Europe and Latin America, and I have found a good representation of people direct from Canada in those offices.

I notice there are only two trade commissioner offices in all of Canada, one of which is at St. John's, Newfoundland, and the other at Vancouver. I notice that the amount for the Vancouver office is being increased this year by a little over $1,000, while the amount for the St. John's office is being reduced by about $6,200. I presume

Supply-Trade and Commerce the difference is in connection with the director. Is it the intention to replace him? I understand he died.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that we used to refer to Newfoundland as a foreign country, or rather as a sister member of the commonwealth. Now it is part of Canada. We are bringing the office down to the point where it is merely a representation of the service in Newfoundland. Vancouver is in a somewhat different position, although I think the duties are about the same. Vancouver is the gateway for everything that comes across the Pacific.
St. John's is in the same position for everything coming across the Atlantic.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: But they do not all stop there; many ships pass by.
It is not intended to replace the director?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

In recent years I have noticed that when a trade commissioner is on leave he visits various centres and addresses local organizations. I think this is an excellent thing. I have heard very favourable comment on this practice by people who are interested in the trade commissioner service. What is the policy of the department in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Trade commissioners are
brought back to Canada every three or four years and are required to make a tour of the country to get in touch with industry, public bodies and so on. This serves a double purpose. First, it makes sure that the trade commissioner is in close touch with Canada and, second, it makes sure that Canadians have an opportunity to meet our representatives and gain from them any information that they may require about the different foreign markets.

One is glad to have an opportunity to pay a tribute, not only to the importance of the trade commissioner service but to the high quality of men who are serving Canada in that very important capacity. It has been my good fortune to meet a number of these men and it is my opinion that they are eminently worthy representatives of Canada in the important posts which they hold.
There is an item in the details on page 487, acquisition of building for residence abroad, $40,000, which is a new item. Could the minister explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We have just sent a man to Djakarta in Indonesia and the report is that there is absolutely no available accommoda-


tion. We regard it as an important key point in the east and this appropriation is to enable the trade commissioner to build or buy a suitable building.
Will the building be used as an office or residence or both? Will it provide living accommodation for anyone but the trade commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It will be a residence and office for the trade commissioner, and if he has an assistant I assume that he will also find room in the building.
How many people are there on the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Just the one.
Just the commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Will it be a case of sending materials there or will materials be acquired in Indonesia for the purpose of constructing this building?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We will not send materials there; the building will be of the type that is built in that city. He will attempt to buy, but if he cannot buy at a favourable price he will arrange to build. If he builds, it will be done with local materials and labour.

What is the policy of the department with reference to the provision of buildings to house the trade commissioner service abroad? Is it the policy to obtain office accommodation in an office building and then leave the commissioner to find his own housing accommodation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the procedure. We rent suitable office space and the staff look after their own housing. Of course where we have an ambassador the trade commissioner is able to obtain office space in the chancellery. Where the trade commissioner is working by himself, he rents an office and finds himself a house.
I take it that this item represents a quite unusual situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. The situation was carefully explored and we were told that there is no possibility of renting accommodation there, either for use as an office or a home.
In what respect is the service at Detroit being augmented? I notice that both the staff and the appropriation are much larger than last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Formerly this was an external affairs office, with a consular officer. We have taken over the staff as a combined trade and consular office.

I think this is the item which deals with advertising. Anything I shall say is not intended to be criticism of the trade commissioners, because I have as high regard for them as any hon. member in the house. I have had the opportunity of meeting Canadian trade commissioners in different countries, and I know they are doing a wonderful job.
However, I do not think we advertise our goods enough. I do not want to take up time because I realize it is getting late in the session. Take the item of hogs alone. I was in Great Britain not long ago, and I have been there many times before. When they sell you a breakfast there they tell you that you are getting a piece of American bacon. That just sticks in my throat when they tell me that it is American bacon, because I know perfectly well it is Canadian bacon.
I have made a study of our bacon in Britain. We have the finest bacon going to Britain, but we do not advertise it. When it is sent away from here it is stamped "product of Canada", but with the fine slicing they did in the United Kingdom during the war that bacon lost its identity completely. I suggest that we follow the pattern set by New Zealand. Right up to the time a man gets New Zealand butter on his table there is a wrapper around it which states that it is a product of New Zealand. Why do we not do that with our bacon? We could supply them with the paper wrapping, telling them that it was the best bacon they could buy, that it was from Canada.
I have seen Canadian eggs in London marked as new-laid eggs when it took ten days to send them there. Stamped on the end of each egg was "product of Canada". It was identified. We send apples there and they are identified as being the product of British Columbia, of the maritimes or of Ontario.
One of the finest products we have ever exported from this country is Canadian bacon. Let us identify our Canadian bacon and not take the dirt that we are eating American bacon when we are served bacon in Great Britain. I made a study of this during the war, and I know we have the finest bacon going to the United Kingdom. Even Danish bacon could not compare with it. I hope the minister will take that into consideration and do something about advertising our products. If you do not toot your own horn nobody will do it for you.

Board of grain commissioners-
440.	Administration, $208,577.

With regard to item 440, board of grain commissioners, it is customary for the board each year to issue an annual report in the month of January and for it to be tabled in the house here by the minister. This year they have not issued that report or, if they have given it to the minister, it has not been printed and distributed. I would like to get some information from the minister with regard to it.
While I am speaking on this matter I would like to point out to the minister that the present board of grain commissioners is short one member. Mr. Milner, who was the third member on the board, has been acting as transport controller for almost two years. This is an important body as far as western producers of grain are concerned and I know they are anxious for the board to have its full membership. I do not know whether it is because the board is short a member that its annual report has not been issued, or whether there are some other reasons.
There is another matter which I should like to raise and the minister can deal with it when he is speaking. I refer to a finding of the board of grain commissioners which was made this year with regard to what is known as the Kreutzweiser case. Under the Canada Grain Act, in the province of Saskatchewan it was always understood by the producers that when grain was offered for sale at an elevator, if the grain was in good condition and the elevator had room for that grain, it was compulsory for the elevator company to purchase the grain. If there was disagreement between the seller and the buyer with regard to the grain, an interim cash ticket would be issued to the seller of the grain and a sample would be taken and sent to the inspection department at Winnipeg. When a final grade was established by the grading department there, an adjustment would be made to the grower on the basis of the interim cash ticket which had been issued to him.
The finding of the board of grain commissioners with regard to this case was that it was not compulsory on the part of the elevator company to issue the interim cash ticket and, unless there is an agreement between the seller and the buyer, it is not compulsory for the elevator company to purchase the grain. That is something which has alarmed a fairly large number of farmers in western Canada. They feel that the interpretation of the Canada Grain Act by the board of grain commissioners in this case takes away certain rights which they as growers in western Canada thought they had under the act. I
23, 1953
Supply-Trade and Commerce would like the minister to say something with regard to this matter.
At a meeting of the agriculture committee last year the minister said that if the growers in western Canada believed there were certain changes which should be made in the act, an opportunity would be given at this session of parliament for them to present their case before the agriculture committee. The committee has not been called and it looks now, at this stage of the session, as though it would be pretty well impossible to call the committee to deal with those matters. I think some explanation is due the producers as to just why these matters have not been referred to the agriculture committee and as to what the government's intention is with regard to the board of grain commissioners and the appointment of another commissioner to bring the board to full strength.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should say at once that the fact that copies of the report of the board of grain commissioners are not available to the house is no fault of that board. That report was forwarded to Ottawa and delivered to the queen's printer prior to March 1. We have been pressing for it ever since, and we are now told that we may get it next Monday. It is only one of several reports that have been held up; one which has been before the queen's printer for a long time was tabled here today in manuscript form. As my hon. friend knows, we are building a new print shop which we hope will be more adequate; but there is nothing a department can do about a report that is delayed by the queen's printer. Apparently the queen's printer is an independent soul.
As far as the board of grain commissioners is concerned, we have three able grain commissioners who comprise the full quota of the board. One of them has been doing extra duty as transport controller, but we hope he can be relieved of these duties this autumn if the pressure which requires a transport controller is relieved. The work of the board is not suffering because that member spends part of his time with the board and part as transport controller.
In connection with the Kreutzweiser case, that is a judicial ruling of the board and I do not know that I want to open it up. I think my hon. friend can see the practical difficulties for an elevator operating close to capacity, with every bin in use, taking in a car of wheat which the elevator operator says is No. 3 northern but which the owner claims is No. 2 northern. The operator must put it in a bin with either one grade or the other. Which bin is he going to choose? He cannot take it in unless he has a special bin to hold
4322	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce it until the grade is officially determined and he can put it in the proper bin.
I do not know what my hon. Mend wants to gain by calling the agriculture committee and discussing that particular case. If the man is not satisfied let him go to the courts. The ruling has been given by the proper authority, but there is always an appeal to the courts.

The ruling at least changes the interpretation which the producers had of certain sections of the Canada Grain Act. If the interpretation of the section is to be that which the board of grain commissioners has given in this case I for one feel that the Canada Grain Act should be amended to give the producers the protection which until this ruling was made they believed they had under the act.

On that point, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister or any officials in the department or the law officers of the crown have given any study to the board's ruling in regard to that section of the Canada Grain Act, section 112. I think the ruling in effect removes the section from the act. I do not know how this man would refer it to the courts, and he might have to go to a lot of expense.
If the minister will think of the experience farmers have had in the past under this section of the Canada Grain Act I believe he will agree that it has been a valuable section. In the past if a farmer went into an elevator with a load of grain and there was a dispute over the grade, the elevator man said he could take it only subject to grade in dock as provided by the Canada Grain Act. A special receptacle was provided, a sample of the grain was placed in it and sent to the chief inspector. When the grade came back the elevator man issued a cash ticket and the grain was sold.
It is certainly not going to help the marketing of grain if an elevator agent can turn away a farmer because there is a dispute over the grade. Most farmers dispute over the grade with the elevator agent every fall. Every farmer wants one grade over that which is offered, and the act has been a protection not only to the growers but to the elevator companies. They really get a referee to decide the grade through provisions in the act for sending it to the chief inspector; but if I read the ruling correctly it removes all the protection which the producers had in that regard.
I think the minister should give some consideration to the ruling, and to the way the act has operated in thie past. Let us not decide whether Mr. Kreutzweiser was right or the


board of grain commissioners' ruling was right. Let us try to decide in what position the producer is placed right now. Let us try to decide whether it is the same position that prevailed in the past, and whether he can sell his grain subject to provisions of grade and dockage.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told that the particular elevator to which he took his grain did not have an empty bin. There were other elevators in the area that did have empty bins, and he was told to take his grain where he could get a specific bin until the grade and dockage were taken. You can pass any law, but if an elevator is completely full of grain and a bin cannot be allotted then the elevator company cannot comply with the law. This is a case where they could not take any of this grain without knowing which particular bin it should go into, because all they had was partially filled bins.

Item 57 is the departmental administration item, Mr. Chairman, and there are quite a number of things which I think one should say, particularly about immigration. I know that the other day in connection with the citizenship act, there were one or two things which the minister suggested we might leave for his estimates.
I think it should be pointed out that, in connection with immigration itself, there has not really been a full-scale discussion of the subject for a number of years. Last year, when we had the revised Immigration Act before the house, the minister took the position that it was merely a revision and consolidation and that it introduced no new policy. Therefore when we got into the details of the act, while I will not say that we were not allowed to discuss policy, I will say that certainly we were discouraged from doing so since, as the minister himself pointed out, the act merely lays down the broad limits within which the government determines policy largely by way of regulation. Then again, the minister's estimates last year were not introduced into the house until even closer to the end of the session than they are on this occasion. Hence there was only a limited discussion of the subject of immigration.
There are, I think, a number of things in connection with immigration which are causing some concern at the present time. This concern is felt in two directions. There are those who are concerned lest there should be an over-generous policy with respect to the admission of immigrants, and there are others who feel that the country is not meeting its full responsibility in the admission of persons from countries which are less fortunate than we are. Then I think there is some considerable concern over the apparently limited usefulness of the assisted passage scheme, particularly with respect to its application to immigrants from the United Kingdom.
There are also certain questions with regard to the position of those who have been admitted to Canada from India, who have been for some time Canadian citizens and who wish to bring their relatives into this country in order to help them on their farms or in their lumber mills which they own in considerable numbers on the Pacific coast. These people want to get their relatives in to help them in those enterprises; yet they find that, although Canadian citizens, they are subject to a quota which prevents them from getting their relatives in. They feel that they are subjected to a great degree of discrimination.

As they pointed out to the minister last year and as, of course, they point out to those of us who come from that province when we are back home, they came here in some cases up to 30 or 40 years ago. Many of them were born here, have been Canadian citizens for all that length of time, yet they cannot bring in their brothers, cousins, or nephews except in extremely limited circumstances and within the over-all limitation of a quota; whereas others who have come to Canada in the last five years, just long enough to acquire Canadian citizenship, have acquired citizenship and are allowed to bring in their relatives as of right.
Those citizens out there feel that prohibition to be a harsh degree of discrimination. I think they have a good case. I must confess that I am unable to find any flaw in it. It seems to me to be a matter where the restrictions should be relaxed on the admission of relatives of those who are Canadian citizens of substance.
These and a number of other problems on which I have not yet touched seem to me to call for a statement by the minister on the policy of this government with respect to immigration. Particularly in the light of the fact, as I said at the beginning, that we have not had a full-scale discussion on immigration for at least two years, I hope the minister will take this occasion this evening to take the committee and the country into his confidence and say what is the policy of the government with respect to immigration and what are their views as to what should be done about immigration in the future.

The figures for immigration into Canada in 1952 showed several very definite trends and of particular interest, perhaps, will be the substantial increase in the numbers coming here from the United Kingdom. Out of a total of 164,498 new arrivals, 42,675 were British. This represents an increase of 36 per cent in the proportion of British immigrants over the previous year, and in actual numbers an increase of more than 11,000 over 1951.
This increase reflects primarily, perhaps, the increasing interest in Canada overseas but it also reflects the work of our officers in the United Kingdom; and in this connection I must pay tribute to the conscientious way in which they are carrying out their duties. There is scarcely a night during the year that Canadian immigration officials are not holding meetings in the smaller towns and cities of Great Britain, outlining the developments that have taken place in this country and showing

films and film strips on life and work in Canada.
I should, however, make reference here to the situation which may face us this year. Transportation of immigrants from the United Kingdom has almost constantly presented a problem. This year, because of the coronation, that problem will be intensified. Hon. members may have noticed an item in the press recently which indicated that, up until the present time, approximately 8,000 Canadians have booked passage to Britain; and that total, of course, is expected to grow. A very considerable number of United States citizens are planning holidays to coincide with the coronation as well.
All these travellers to the United Kingdom have, of course, booked their return passage, which means that westward transportation following the coronation will be very difficult to secure. We are seeking ways in which this

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
problem may be lessened, but I am not hopeful that any substantial increase in accommodation will be available although we shall continue to seek ways and means to provide for those people who wish to migrate here.
Hon. members, of course, will have noted that the 1952 figures show a decrease from the 194,000 who came to Canada in 1951. I should explain in this connection that there were some unusual circumstances in 1951. It was, first of all, a year in which Canada's absorptive capacity was extremely high. The second factor was that a great deal of shipping became available in the final months of the year, partly due to the fact that the international refugee organization was winding up its activities and still had ships under charter. These things helped to bring us a very heavy intake in the final months. As a matter of fact in October, November and December of 1951 new arrivals came to Canada at an average rate of approximately 21,500 each month. That did not occur in 1952.
Another trend to which I would like to call the attention of hon. members is the way in which the flow of immigrants came to Canada during 1952. And in referring to this I would like to draw attention to two things that are elementary in carrying out an immigration program for a country such as Canada. The first of these is that the best time for workers to arrive is in the spring, summer and early fall. The second is that the integration of any immigrant is speeded if he has his family around him.
It was apparent that 1952 would not offer as many opportunities for immigrants all through the year as did 1951. For instance, the demand for additional workers in heavy construction, in the mines and in the forests was not expected to be as great as in 1951. Our program, therefore, envisaged the movement of as high a proportion of workers as possible during the early months of the year, with priority given to dependents in the final months.
As a result, in the first six months of last year the new arrivals were almost 20,000 in excess of the same six months in the big year of 1951. In the final months of the year, while the number of arrivals was substantial, we find the objective of reunion of families being achieved, with the number of dependents in each of the final three months of the year exceeding the number of those coming here as workers. The figures were 15,616 dependents and 11,944 workers.
We find, too, that the workers were going into immediate employment. For instance, on January 3 of this year we had only a negligible number, all single men, awaiting placement in our reception centres across Canada.

For instance, during the past few weeks our officers in the province of Quebec have been holding short courses in Canadian agricultural methods for newcomers. Approximately 50 French-speaking new Canadians have been attending this course at St. Johns, Quebec, and I am happy to state that every one of these 50 is on a farm of his own, that he is making progress, finding Canadian farming a good way of life and seeing here an opportunity for his children to maintain the Canadian tradition of the family farm.
All in all we have been getting an exceedingly fine type of immigrant, with the vast majority coming from those countries whose people have demonstrated in the past that they integrate well into Canadian communities and fit themselves quickly to accept the full responsibility of citizenship.
When we consider immigration I believe most of us think primarily in terms of workers. It is true that workers make up something more than 50 per cent of the intake, but we should not lose sight of the fact that dependents are also represented in substantial numbers. Of last year's arrivals approximately 85,000 were workers; the remainder, more than 79,000 dependent wives, children and parents. As a matter of record, almost one out of every four who came to Canada in 1952 was a child 14 years of age or younger. Again I suggest that this is a healthy characteristic of the Canadian immigration program.
We had in 1952 a 20 per cent increase in the number coming here from the United States. And along with the increased flow of United States citizens coming to Canada

Part of this is undoubtedly due to the flattering publicity Canada is receiving south of the border, publicity of the great development in this country, and of a healthy climate for investment and enterprise.
And now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to take just a very brief look at the future. The government is fully aware that Canada needs more people, that we cannot fulfil our destiny and develop our resources with a population of only a little more than fourteen and a half million. The government is fully aware that natural increase will not alone provide the population we must have. The government is aware also of the fact that the difficult times we had in the 1930's had an effect on the natural increase and the number of Canadians reaching working age is lower than normal at the present time. Accordingly the government will continue its program of immigration to stimulate Canadian growth and Canadian development.
To give effect to this, we are now selecting immigrants on a very wide basis. First priority, of course, is being given in all countries to the movement of close relatives of people already established in Canada. I believe hon. members will agree with this. However, the close relatives are only a percentage of those we are selecting now. For instance, in all countries where we have immigration offices, outside of Asia, we are selecting, in addition to the close relatives, anyone who meets our qualifications and for whom there are opportunities in Canada. There is one exception to the above; that is in the Netherlands, with which country we have an agreement for the selection of immigrants. In those countries where we have no immigration offices we are able to deal only with cases of close relatives and cases of exceptional merit.
The approach will continue to be a realistic one, with the development of our economy the guiding factor. We shall anticipate future developments as closely as we can and gear our immigration program to them, realizing as we do that the next few years will present greater opportunities for the growth of the Canadian nation than ever before, and that under these circumstances there is an obligation on the government to seize the opportunity and make the maximum use of it, not only in the interests of our people but in the interests of peace.
